What will that day be, when Mary, the mother of the Lord, will come to meet you, attended by choirs of virgins; when, after the Red Sea and Pharaoh drowned with his army, holding the timbrel she will lead the chant for those who answer: \"Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously magnified. The horse and his rider he has cast into the sea\"? Then Thecla will fly joyful into your embraces. Then the Bridegroom himself will come to meet you and say: \"Rise, come, my neighbour, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone.\" Then the angels will marvel and say: \"Who is this that looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?\" The daughters will see you and praise you, and the queens and concubines will proclaim you blessed. Then another choir of chastity will come to meet you: Sarah will come with the married, Anna the daughter of Phanuel with the widows. They will be, as in different flocks, the mothers of your flesh and of your spirit. The one will rejoice that she bore you; the other will exult that she taught you. Then truly the Lord will mount upon the ass and enter the heavenly Jerusalem. Then the little ones, of whom the Saviour speaks in Isaiah, \"Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me,\" lifting up the palms of victory, will sing with one voice: \"Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest.\" Then the hundred and forty-four thousand will hold harps before the throne and the elders, and will sing a new song, and no one will be able to know that song except the appointed number: \"These are they who have not defiled themselves with women — for they have remained virgins; these are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.\" As often as the empty ambition of the world delights you, as often as you see anything glorious in the world, pass over in your mind to paradise; begin to be what you will be, and you will hear from your Bridegroom: \"Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm,\" and, fortified in deed and mind alike, you will cry out: \"Many waters cannot quench love, and rivers shall not cover it.\"

1. You ask me, dearest Nepotian — you ask in letters from across the sea, and ask repeatedly — to set out for you in a short book the precepts of living, and to show by what method a man who has left the world's military service and begun to be either a monk or a cleric may hold to the straight path of Christ and not be swept aside into the various byways of the vices. When I was a young man — indeed, almost a boy — and was reining in the first onsets of a wanton age by the hardship of the desert, I wrote to your uncle, the holy Heliodorus, a letter of exhortation, full of tears and complaints, such as might show the feeling of a deserted companion. But in that work I played the part of my years, and, while still warm with the studies and teachings of the rhetoricians, I painted certain things with the flower of the schools. Now my head is white and my brow lined, and the dewlaps hang from my chin like an ox's:
The chill blood stiffens around my heart;

and so the same poet sings elsewhere:
Time bears away all things, the mind as well;
and shortly after:
Now so many songs are gone from my memory, and even my voice fails Moeris.

2. But that I may not seem to draw this only from heathen literature, learn also the mysteries of the sacred volumes. David, at seventy years of age, once a warlike man, could not be warmed in the chill of his old age. So a girl is sought from all the borders of Israel, Abishag the Shunammite, that she might sleep with the king and warm his aged body. Does it not seem to you, if you follow the surface of the letter, either a fiction out of a mime or the buffoonery of the Atellan farces? A chilled old man is wrapped in clothing, and grows warm only in the embrace of youth. Bathsheba was still living, Abigail still survived, and the rest of his wives and concubines whom Scripture records: all of them are passed over as though they too were cold, and the old man warms in the embraces of one alone. Abraham was far older than David, and yet, while Sarah lived, he sought no other wife; Isaac was twice David's years, and never grew cold with Rebecca, though she was now old; I say nothing of the men before the flood, who, after nine hundred years, with limbs not merely aged but almost decayed, by no means sought the embraces of girls; Moses, certainly, the leader of the people of Israel, was a hundred and twenty years old, and did not exchange Zipporah for another.

3. Who, then, is this Shunammite, a wife and a virgin so fervent that she warmed the cold, so holy that she did not provoke the warmed man to lust? Let the wisest Solomon set forth his father's delight, and let the man of peace tell of the warrior's embraces: Get wisdom, get understanding. Forget it not, neither decline from the words of my mouth, neither forsake her, and she will lay hold of you; love her, and she will keep you. The beginning of wisdom: get wisdom, and in all your getting get understanding; embrace her, and she will exalt you; honour her, and she will encompass you, that she may give to your head a crown of graces, and may protect you with a crown of delights.
Almost all the powers of the body are altered in the old, and while wisdom alone increases, the rest decrease: fastings, sleeping on the ground, running here and there, the receiving of strangers, the defence of the poor, perseverance in standing at prayer, the visiting of the sick, the labour of the hands by which alms are supplied, and — that I may not draw out my discourse too far — everything that is performed through the body grows less as the body breaks down. Nor do I say this as though wisdom grew cold in the young and those still of firmer age — at least in those who have pursued knowledge through labour and the most ardent zeal, through holiness of life too and frequency of prayer to God — wisdom that withers with age in most of the old; but rather that youth endures many wars of the body, and amid the incentives of the vices and the ticklings of the flesh is choked, like fire in greener wood, and cannot unfold its full radiance. But old age — again I remind you — in those who have furnished their youth with honourable arts and have meditated in the law of the Lord day and night, grows more learned with age, more practised by use, wiser with the passage of time, and reaps the sweetest fruits of its old studies.
And so that wise man of Greece, when, having completed a hundred and seven years, he saw that he was about to die, is said to have grieved that he was then leaving life just when he had begun to be wise; Plato died in his eighty-first year, pen in hand; Isocrates filled out ninety-nine years in the labour of teaching and writing; I say nothing of the other philosophers — Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, Cleanthes — who flourished in the studies of wisdom when already of great age: I come to the poets, Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, Stesichorus, who, far advanced in years, with death near, sang some swan-song sweeter than their wont. Sophocles, when on account of his extreme old age and the neglect of his household affairs he was accused of madness by his sons, recited to the judges the tragedy of Oedipus which he had lately written, and gave so great a proof of wisdom in his now-broken age that he turned the severity of the tribunal into the applause of the theatre. Nor is this any wonder, since even Cato, the most eloquent of the Roman race, when already a censor and an old man, neither blushed at nor despaired of learning Greek letters. Homer, certainly, relates that from the tongue of Nestor, now aged and almost decrepit, speech flowed sweeter than honey.
But the mystery of the very name Abishag indicates the fuller wisdom of the old. For it is interpreted "my father is superabundant," or "the roaring of my father." The word "superabundant" is ambiguous, and in the present passage signifies virtue, in that wisdom in the old is fuller and overflowing and lavish; but in another passage "superabundant" is put for "superfluous," as not necessary. "Sag," that is, "roaring," is properly so named when the waves of the sea resound, and, so to speak, the roar coming from the deep is heard. By this it is shown that the most abundant thunder of the divine word, beyond the human voice, abides in the old. Furthermore, "Shunammite" in our tongue is rendered "scarlet," to signify that wisdom is warm and glows with divine reading; which, though it points to the mystery of the Lord's blood, nevertheless also shows the fervour of wisdom. And so that midwife in Genesis binds the scarlet thread upon the hand of Pharez, who, from the fact that he had divided the wall that separated two peoples before him, received the name of the "divider," that is, Pharez. And Rahab the harlot, as a type of the Church, let down the little cord that contained the mysteries of the blood, that she might be saved at the destruction of Jericho. And in another passage Scripture records concerning holy men: These are the Kenites who came from the warmth of the house of Rechab. And our Lord in the Gospel: I have come, he says, to send fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled! It was this fire, kindled in the hearts of the disciples, that compelled them to say: Did not our heart burn within us while he spoke on the way and opened to us the Scriptures?

4. To what end has all this been recalled in so long a preface? That you may not seek from me boyish declamations, little flowers of maxims, the allurements of words, and at the close of each chapter certain pointed and briefly concluded turns of phrase, such as rouse the applause and shouts of the hearers. Let wisdom alone embrace me, and let our Abishag, who never grows old, rest in my bosom. She is unpolluted and of perpetual virginity, and, after the likeness of Mary, since she daily brings forth and is ever in travail, she is uncorrupted. From this, I think, the Apostle too said that he was "fervent in spirit," and the Lord proclaimed in the Gospel that at the end of the world, when, according to the prophet Zechariah, a foolish shepherd shall arise, wisdom shall decrease and the love of many shall grow cold. Hear me, then — as blessed Cyprian says — words not eloquent but strong. Hear a brother by fellowship, a father by age, who would lead you from the cradle of faith to the perfect age, and who, in laying down precepts for living through each of its degrees, may through you instruct others as well. I know indeed that from your uncle, the blessed Heliodorus, who is now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned the things that are holy and learn them daily, and have the example of his virtues as your rule of life; but receive also my own contributions, such as they are, and join this little book to his, so that, while he has trained you as a monk, this may teach you to be a perfect cleric.

5. Therefore let the cleric who serves the Church of Christ first interpret his own title, and, having set the definition of the name before him, strive to be what he is called. For if kleros in Greek is called sors ("lot") in Latin, clerics are so named either because they are of the Lord's lot, or because the Lord himself is the lot — that is, the portion — of the clerics. Now he who is either himself a portion of the Lord, or has the Lord as his portion, ought so to conduct himself that he both possesses the Lord and is himself possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the prophet, "The Lord is my portion," can have nothing apart from the Lord; for if he have anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he have gold, if silver, if possessions, if various furnishings — with such portions the Lord does not deign to become his portion. But if I am a portion of the Lord and the cord of his inheritance, and receive no portion among the rest of the tribes, but, like a Levite and a priest, live by the tithes and, serving the altar, am sustained by the offering of the altar — having food and clothing, with these I shall be content, and naked I shall follow the naked cross. I beseech you, then, and, repeating it again and again, I shall warn you, not to think the office of the clergy a kind of the old military service — that is, not to seek the world's gains in the warfare of Christ, not to have more than when you began to be a cleric, lest it be said to you: Their portions shall not profit them. Let the poor and strangers, and with them Christ, know your little table as their guest; flee like a kind of plague a cleric turned trader, made rich from poor, made glorious from low-born. Evil conversations corrupt good manners. You despise gold, another loves it; you trample on riches, he pursues them; silence, gentleness, seclusion are dear to your heart, but to him wordiness, a brazen brow, the marketplaces, the public squares, and the doctors' shops are pleasing: amid so great a discord of manners, what concord can there be?

Let women's feet rarely or never enter your little lodging. Either be equally ignorant of all maidens and virgins of Christ, or love them equally. Do not stay under the same roof; do not trust in your past chastity. You cannot be holier than David nor wiser than Solomon; remember always that a woman cast the dweller of paradise out of his possession. When you are sick, let some holy brother attend you, or a sister, or a mother, or any woman of approved faith in the eyes of all. But if there be no persons of such kinship and chastity, the Church maintains many old women who may both render service and receive a benefit by ministering, so that even your sickness may have the fruit of almsgiving. I know of some who have recovered in body and begun to sicken in soul. She ministers to you at peril whose face you frequently regard. If, on account of the clerical office, you visit a widow or a virgin, never enter the house alone, and keep such companions as will not bring you into disrepute by their company. If a reader, an acolyte, or a singer follows you, let them be adorned not with clothing but with character, nor let them curl their hair with a curling-iron, but let them promise chastity by their dress. Do not sit alone and without a witness with a woman alone. If something more private must be said, she has a nurse, the elder virgin of the house, a widow, a married woman; she is not so unsociable as to have no one but you to whom she would dare to confide. Beware of all suspicions, and whatever can plausibly be invented, avoid beforehand, that it may not be invented. Holy love has no place for frequent little gifts, napkins and garters and garments laid to the mouth, tasted morsels, and coaxing, sweet little notes. "My honey, my light, my desire," and the other follies of lovers, all the dalliances and charms and laughable refinements — these we blush at in comedies, we detest in men of the world: how much more in clerics, and in clerics who are monks, whose priesthood is adorned by their profession and whose profession by their priesthood! Nor do I say this because I fear such things in you or in holy men, but because in every profession, in every rank and sex, both good men and bad are found, and the condemnation of the worse is the praise of the good.

6. I am ashamed to say it: the priests of idols, mime-actors and charioteers and harlots receive inheritances; to clerics and monks alone this is forbidden by law — and forbidden not by persecutors but by Christian emperors. Nor do I complain of the law, but I grieve that we have deserved this law. A cautery is a good thing, but what is the wound that I should need a cautery? The provision of the law is foresighted and stern, and yet not even thus is avarice restrained. By trusts we mock the laws, and, as though the decrees of emperors were greater than those of Christ, we fear the laws and despise the Gospels. Let there be an heir, but the mother of her sons — that is, the Church, the mother of his flock — who bore them, nourished them, and fed them. Why do we thrust ourselves between mother and children? It is the glory of a bishop to provide for the needs of the poor; it is the shame of all priests to study their own riches. Born in a poor house and in a country hut, I who could scarcely fill my roaring belly with millet and coarse bread now turn up my nose at fine flour and honey; I know the kinds and the names of fishes, on what shore a shellfish was gathered; by their flavour I distinguish the provinces of birds, and at last the very rarity of foods and their cost delight me.
I hear, moreover, of the shameful servility of some men toward childless old men and women. They themselves set out the chamber-pot, they besiege the bed, and with their own hands they take up the corrupt matter of the stomach and the phlegm of the lungs. They tremble at the entrance of the physician, and with quivering lips ask whether the patient is better; and if the old man grows a little stronger, they are in peril, and with feigned gladness the mind within is tortured with avarice. For they fear lest they lose their service, and they compare the long-lived old man to the years of Methuselah. Oh, how great would be the reward with the Lord, if he hoped for no present price! With what great sweats is a vain inheritance sought! With less labour Christ's pearl might have been bought.

7. Read the divine Scriptures often — indeed, let the sacred reading never be laid down from your hands. Learn what you may teach; hold fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine, that you may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to convince the gainsayers. Continue in the things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you have learned them, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason of the hope that is in you. Let not your works confound your speech, lest, when you speak in the church, anyone silently reply: "Why, then, do you not do these things yourself?" He is a dainty master who, with full belly, disputes about fastings; even a thief can accuse avarice; let the mind and the mouth of Christ's priest agree.
Be subject to your bishop, and look up to him as to the parent of your soul: to love is the part of sons, to fear the part of servants. "And if I am a father," he says, "where is my honour? And if I am a master, where is my fear?" In the same man you have more than one name to regard: monk, bishop, uncle. But let bishops too know that they are priests, not lords: let them honour clerics as clerics, that they too may be reverenced by clerics as bishops. There is a witty saying of the orator Domitius: "Shall I," he says, "hold you as a chief, when you do not hold me as a senator?" What Aaron and his sons were, that let us understand the bishop and the presbyters to be: one Lord, one temple, let there be also one ministry. Let them always recall what the apostle Peter enjoins upon priests: Feed the flock of the Lord which is among you, taking care of it not by constraint, but willingly, according to God; not for the sake of base gain, but freely; not as lording it over the clergy, but being made an example to the flock from the heart, so that, when the chief of the shepherds shall appear, you may receive the unfading crown of glory. It is a most wretched custom in certain churches for the presbyters to keep silent, and not to speak when the bishops are present, as though the bishops either envied them or did not deign to hear them. "And if anything," says the apostle Paul, "be revealed to another that sits by, let the first hold his peace. For you may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn and all may be comforted. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets: for God is not the God of dissension, but of peace." A wise son is the glory of his father; let the bishop rejoice in his own judgment, when he has chosen such priests for Christ.

8. When you speak in church, let it be not the shout of the people but their groaning that is roused; let the tears of your hearers be your praise. Let the discourse of the presbyter be seasoned by the reading of the Scriptures. I would not have you a declaimer and a brawler and a babbler, but skilled in the mystery and most learned in the sacraments of your God. To roll out words and, by the swiftness of speaking, to win admiration from an unskilled crowd is the mark of ignorant men. A brazen brow often expounds what it does not know, and, when it has persuaded others, claims knowledge for itself as well. My teacher once, Gregory of Nazianzus, when I asked him to explain what was meant in Luke by the "second-first" Sabbath — that is, the secundoprimum — gracefully jested: "I will teach you," he said, "about this matter in church, where, with all the people applauding me, you will be compelled against your will to know what you do not know; or else, if you alone keep silent, you alone will be condemned by all for folly." Nothing is so easy as to deceive a cheap little crowd and an unlearned assembly by a glib tongue, for whatever it does not understand it admires the more. Marcus Tullius — of whom that most beautiful tribute was made: "Demosthenes took from you the being the first orator; you took from him the being the only one" — mark what he says in his oration for Quintus Gallius about the favour of the crowd and about unskilled speakers: "But at these games — for I speak of what I have myself lately experienced — a certain poet holds sway, a man very lettered, whose are those banquets of poets and philosophers, when he makes Euripides and Menander dispute with each other, and in another place Socrates and Epicurus, whose ages we know were separated not by years but by centuries. And how great is the applause and the shouting that he stirs! For he has many fellow-pupils in the theatre who likewise never learned their letters."

9. Avoid dark garments as much as white; finery and squalor are alike to be shunned, since the one savours of luxury, the other of vainglory. Not to go about without a linen cloak, but to have no money for linen garments, is praiseworthy; otherwise it is ridiculous and full of disgrace to boast, with a full purse, that you have no handkerchief or napkin. There are some who give little to the poor that they may receive more, and under the pretext of almsgiving seek riches; this is rather to be called hunting than almsgiving. Thus are wild beasts, thus birds, thus fishes caught: a little bait is set upon the hook, that the purses of matrons may be drawn out upon it. The bishop, to whom the church is entrusted, knows whom to set over the distribution and care of the poor. It is better not to have what I might give than shamelessly to beg. But it is also a kind of arrogance to wish to seem more merciful than the bishop of Christ. We cannot all do all things. One in the church is an eye, another a tongue, another a hand, another a foot, another an ear, a belly, and the rest. Read Paul to the Corinthians: diverse members make up one body. Let not the unlettered and merely simple brother therefore think himself holy if he knows nothing, nor let the skilled and eloquent in speech reckon his eloquence holiness. Of the two imperfect things, it is far better to have a holy rusticity than a sinful eloquence.

10. Many build walls and lay down columns for the church: the marbles gleam, the panelled ceilings glitter with gold, the altar is set with gems — and yet there is no choosing of Christ's ministers. Nor let anyone object to me the wealthy temple in Judaea, the table, the lamps, the censers, the dishes, the cups, the little mortars, and the rest skilfully wrought of gold. These things were approved by the Lord then, when the priests sacrificed victims and the blood of beasts was the redemption of sins — though all these things had gone before as a figure. But they were written for our sakes, upon whom the ends of the ages have come; now, however, since a poor Lord has consecrated the poverty of his house, let us think upon the cross, and we shall reckon riches mire. Why do we wonder that Christ calls riches "unrighteous mammon"? Why do we look up to and love what Peter testifies he does not possess? Otherwise, if we follow only the letter, and the plain narrative delights us in gold and riches, let us observe the rest along with the gold: let Christ's bishops marry virgin wives; however good of mind a man be, if he have a scar and is deformed, let him be deprived of the priesthood; let leprosy of the body be preferred to the vices of the soul; let us grow and multiply and replenish the earth; let us neither sacrifice the lamb nor celebrate the mystical Passover, since these are forbidden by law to be done without the temple; let us pitch the tabernacle in the seventh month and sound the solemn fast with the trumpet. But if all these things we should understand spiritually, comparing spiritual with spiritual, and knowing with Paul that the law is spiritual, and singing the words of David, "Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wondrous things of your law," so as to understand even as our Lord himself understood and interpreted the Sabbath, then let us either reject gold along with the rest of the superstitions of the Jews, or, if gold pleases us, let the Jews please us too, whom along with their gold we must either approve or condemn.

11. You must avoid the banquets of worldly men, and especially of those who are swollen with honours. It is shameful that, before the doors of a priest of the crucified and poor Lord — who fed even on borrowed food — the lictors of consuls and soldiers should keep watch, and that the judge of the province should dine better at your house than in the palace. But if you allege that you do these things in order to plead for the wretched and the oppressed: the worldly judge defers more to a self-controlled cleric than to a rich one, and reveres your holiness more than your wealth; or, if he be such a man as will not hear clerics save among the dishes, I shall gladly do without a benefit of this kind, and shall plead with Christ as my judge, who can better come to my aid; for it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man, better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.
Never smell of wine, lest you hear that saying of the philosopher: "This is not to offer a kiss, but to offer a toast." Drunken priests both the Apostle condemns and the old law forbids. They that serve the altar shall not drink wine and strong drink. "Strong drink" in the Hebrew tongue is the name for any drink that can intoxicate, whether it is made with ferment, or fruit-juices are boiled down into a sweet and outlandish drink, or the fruit of palms is pressed into liquor, or a thicker water is strained from cooked grain. Whatever intoxicates and overturns the steadiness of the mind, flee it as you would wine. Nor do I say this so as to condemn a creature of God — since the Lord too is called a wine-drinker, and to Timothy with a sick stomach a little draught of wine was allowed — but we require, in drinking, a measure proportioned to age, to health, and to the constitution of the body. But if without wine I burn — and I burn with youth and am inflamed with the heat of the blood and am of a juicy and vigorous body — I shall gladly do without the cup in which there is the suspicion of poison. It is finely said among the Greeks, though I do not know whether it sounds as well among us: "A fat belly does not beget a fine perception."

12. Impose on yourself only as much fasting as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, not superstitious. What profit is it not to eat oil, and to seek out certain troubles and difficulties of foods? Dried figs, pepper, nuts, the fruit of palms, fine flour, honey, pistachios — the whole cultivation of gardens is harassed, that we may not eat the common bread. I hear, moreover, of some who, against the nature of things and of men, drink no water and eat no bread, but sip dainty little broths and crushed herbs and the juice of beets, not from a cup but from a shell. For shame! Do we not blush at follies of this kind, nor weary of the superstition? Besides, we even seek a reputation for abstinence amid delicacies. The strongest fast is water and bread; but because this has no glory, and we all live on bread and water, it is reckoned, as it were, no public and common fast.

13. Take care that you do not go fowling for the little rumours of men, that you do not exchange an offence against God for the praise of peoples. "If I yet pleased men," says the Apostle, "I should not be the servant of Christ"; he ceased to please men and became a servant of Christ. Through good report and evil, on the right hand and on the left, the soldier of Christ marches; he is neither lifted up by praise nor broken by blame, he is not puffed up by riches, nor cast down by poverty, and he despises both glad things and sad. By day the sun shall not burn him, neither the moon by night. I would not have you pray on the corners of the streets, lest the breath of popular favour break the straight course of your prayers; I would not have you broaden your fringes and, for ostentation, wear pious phylacteries and, with a repugnant conscience, surround yourself with Pharisaic ambition. It is better to carry these things in the heart than on the body, to have God as your supporter, not the gaze of men. Do you wish to know what ornaments the Lord seeks? Have prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude. Be enclosed within these regions of heaven; let this team of four, like a charioteer, bear you, swift, to the goal of Christ. Nothing is more precious than this necklace, nothing more variegated than this variety of gems. On every side you are adorned, girding and protecting; and they are to you both an ornament and a defence: the gems are turned into shields.

14. Take care also that you have neither an itching tongue nor itching ears — that is, neither disparage others yourself, nor listen to others disparaging. "You sat," he says, "and spoke against your brother, and laid a stumbling-block against your mother's son; these things you did, and I was silent. You thought iniquity, that I would be like you; I will reprove you, and set you before your own face." It is to be understood: "Your words, and all that you have spoken of others, that by your own sentence you may be judged, being yourself caught in those very things which you reproved in others." Nor indeed is that a just excuse: "When others report a thing to me, I cannot help doing an injury." No one willingly reports to an unwilling hearer. An arrow is never driven into a stone; sometimes, rebounding, it strikes the one who aimed it. Let the slanderer learn, when he sees that you do not gladly listen, not to slander readily. "With slanderers," says Solomon, "do not mingle, for their destruction shall come suddenly, and the ruin of both, who knows it?" — that is, of him who slanders as well as of him who lends his ear to the slanderer.

15. It is your duty to visit the sick, to know the households, the matrons and their children, and not to be ignorant of the secrets of men of rank. Let it therefore be your duty to keep not only your eyes chaste, but your tongue as well. Never discuss the beauty of women, nor let one household learn through you what is going on in another. Hippocrates binds his disciples by an oath before he teaches them, and compels them to swear in his own words; he extorts silence by a solemn pledge; he prescribes their speech, their gait, their dress, and their manners: how much more ought we, to whom the medicine of souls has been entrusted, to love the households of all Christians as our own. Let them know us rather as comforters in their sorrows than as banqueters in their prosperity. The cleric is easily despised who, often invited to dinner, does not refuse.

16. Let us never accept while asking, and rarely while asked. For somehow even the very man who entreats you to take, when you have taken, judges you the cheaper, and, strange to say, admires you the more if you have scorned his request. A preacher of continence, let him not arrange marriages. He who reads the Apostle, "It remains that they that have wives be as though they had none," why does he compel a virgin to marry? He who is a priest of one marriage, why does he exhort a widow to be twice-married? How can men be the agents and stewards of others' houses and estates, who are bidden to despise their own means? To snatch something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To have received what is to be distributed to the poor, and, while many are starving, to be cautious or timid, or — what is most manifest wickedness — to subtract anything from it, surpasses the cruelty of all robbers. I am tortured with hunger, and do you judge how much is enough for my belly? Either distribute at once what you have received, or, if you are a timid steward, dismiss the giver, that he may himself distribute his own. I would not have your little bag full on my occasion. No one can keep my own better than I can. He is the best steward who reserves nothing for himself.

17. You have compelled me, dearest Nepotian — now that my little book on virginity, which I wrote at Rome for the holy Eustochium, has been stoned — after ten years to open my mouth again at Bethlehem, and to expose myself to be pierced by all men's tongues. For either I ought to have written nothing, that I might not undergo the judgment of men — which you forbade me to do — or, in writing, I ought to know that the darts of all the evil-speakers will be hurled against us. I beseech them to be quiet and to cease their reviling; for we have written not as adversaries but as friends, nor have we inveighed against those who sin, but warned them not to sin. And we have been stern judges not against them only but against ourselves as well, and, wishing to take the mote from another's eye, we have first cast out our own beam. We have injured no one, no one has been so much as marked by description, no one has my speech assailed by name: the discussion of the vices is general. Whoever shall wish to be angry with me first confesses of himself that he is such a man.

1. You implore me in a letter, and entreat me as a suppliant, to write to you — or rather to write back — how you ought to live and to preserve the crown of widowhood with the name of chastity unimpaired. My mind rejoices, my heart leaps, my affection exults that you desire to be, after your husband, what your mother Titiana of holy memory was for a long time while her husband lived. Her prayers and supplications have been heard. She has obtained in her only daughter what she possessed while alive. You have, besides, the great distinction of your family: that from Camillus onward it is written that none — or hardly any — of your house has known a second marriage, so that you are not so much to be praised if you persevere as a widow, as to be cursed if, as a Christian, you do not keep what for so many ages heathen women have preserved.

2. I say nothing of Paula and Eustochium, the flowers of your stock, lest I seem, on the occasion of exhorting you, to be praising them; and I pass over Blesilla, who, following her husband, your kinsman, in a brief span of life fulfilled many seasons of virtue. And would that men imitated the renown of women, and that wrinkled old age rendered what youth offers of its own accord! Knowingly and seeing it, I put my hand into the flame: eyebrows will be drawn up, an arm will be stretched out, and an angry Chremes will rage with swollen mouth. The nobles rise up, and against my letter the patrician throng will thunder, crying out that I am a magician, a seducer, to be carried off to the ends of the earth. Let them add, if they wish, "Samaritan" too, that I may recognize the title of my Lord. Certainly I do not divide a daughter from a parent, nor do I quote that saying of the Gospel: "Let the dead bury their dead." For he lives who believes in Christ, and he who believes in him ought himself to walk as he walked.

3. Let envy depart — that envy which the inborn malice of slanderers ever fastens upon the Christian name, so that, while men fear reproaches, they may not be roused to the virtues. Apart from letters we do not know one another, and there is no cause but that of piety where there is no acquaintance of the flesh. Honour your father, but only so long as he does not separate you from your true Father. Know the bond of blood only so long as he himself acknowledges his Creator; otherwise David will straightway sing to you: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your own people and your father's house; and the King shall desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God. Great is the reward of the parent forgotten: The King shall desire your beauty. Because you have heard, because you have seen, because you have inclined your ear and forgotten your people and your father's house, therefore the King shall desire your beauty and shall say to you: You are all fair, my nearest, and there is no spot in you. What is more beautiful than the soul which is called the daughter of God and seeks no outward ornaments? She believes in Christ and, enriched by this ambition, goes forth to her Bridegroom, having the same one as Lord whom she has as husband.

4. What straits marriage holds you learned in your very marriage, and you were sated to the point of nausea, as if with the flesh of quails. Your throat has tasted the bitterest gall; you have vomited up the sour and sickening food and relieved your seething stomach: why do you wish to take in again what was harmful to you? A dog returning to its vomit, and a sow to its wallowing in the mire. Even the brute beasts and the wandering birds do not fall twice into the same snares and nets. Or do you fear that the offspring of the Furian line should fail, and that your father should have from you no little child to crawl on his breast and smear his neck with filth? Why not? All who have had marriages have children, and all to whom children are born answer to the worth of their kind! Did Cicero's son show his father's image in eloquence? Did your Cornelia, that pattern of chastity and fruitfulness alike, rejoice that she had borne her Gracchi? It is ridiculous to hope as a certainty for what you see that many do not have, and, when they have had it, have lost it. To whom do you bequeath such great riches? To Christ, who cannot die. Whom will you have as heir? Him whom you have also as Lord. Your father will be saddened, but Christ will rejoice; your household will mourn, but the angels will give thanks. Let your father do as he wishes with his own: you belong not to him to whom you were born, but to him to whom you were reborn, and who redeemed you at a great price, with his own blood.

5. Beware of nurses and bearers and wine-loving creatures of that kind, who long to fill their bellies from your skin. They counsel not what profits you but what profits themselves, and often they whine out that verse:
"Will you alone, mourning, waste your perpetual youth, and never know sweet children nor the rewards of love?"
Where there is chastity and holiness, there is frugality; where frugality, there is loss to the servants. Whatever they have not received, they think taken from themselves, nor do they consider how much someone has, but how much they themselves receive; wherever they see a Christian, at once comes that street-cry: "The Greek, the impostor!" These men sow the foulest rumours and pretend to have heard from others what has gone out from themselves, being at once the authors and the magnifiers of it. Thence comes a report born of a lie, which, when it has reached the matrons and has been fanned by their tongues, penetrates the provinces. You may see very many raging with rabid mouth and painted face, with viperish eyes and pumice-smoothed teeth, carping at Christians. Here is some woman,
who has a hyacinth-coloured cloak about her shoulders, mumbling something rancid through her stammering nostrils, and tripping up her words with her dainty palate.
The whole chorus chimes in, and all the benches bark. Men of our own order are joined to them, who are both gnawed at and gnaw — talkative against us, mute on their own behalf — as though they themselves were something other than monks, and as though whatever is said against monks did not redound upon clerics too, who are the fathers of monks. The loss of the flock is the shepherd's disgrace, just as, on the other hand, that monk's life is praised who holds the priests of Christ in veneration and does not disparage the rank by which he was made a Christian.

6. I have said these things, my daughter in Christ, not doubting of your purpose — for you would never have asked for a letter of exhortation if you wavered about the good of a single marriage — but that you might understand the wickedness of the servants who carry you about for sale, the snares of your kinsfolk, and the well-meaning error of your father, to whom, though I grant love toward you, I do not grant knowledge of love, saying with the Apostle: I confess, they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. Imitate rather — for I shall repeat it again and again — your holy mother, of whom, as often as I recall her, there comes to my mind her ardour for Christ, her pallor from fasting, her almsgiving to the poor, her service to the servants of God, her humility both of heart and of dress, and in all things her moderate speech. Let your father — whom I name for honour's sake, not because he is of consular and patrician rank, but because he is a Christian — fulfil his name and rejoice that he has begotten a daughter for Christ, not for the world; nay rather, let him grieve that you have both lost your virginity in vain and lost the fruit of your marriage. Where is the husband whom he gave you? Even had he been lovable, even had he been good, death would have ended everything, and destruction would have dissolved the bond of the flesh. Seize the occasion, I beg, and make a virtue of necessity. In Christians it is not the beginning that is sought, but the end: Paul began ill, but ended well; Judas's beginnings are praised, but his end is condemned for treachery. Read Ezekiel: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him, in whatever day he shall sin, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him, in whatever day he shall turn from his wickedness. This is the ladder of Jacob, by which the angels ascend and descend, on which the Lord leans, stretching out his hand to the fallen and sustaining the weary steps of those who climb by the contemplation of himself. But as he does not will the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn and live, so he hates the lukewarm and they quickly make him sick. To whom more is forgiven, he loves the more.

7. That harlot in the Gospel was saved by being baptized in her own tears and by the hair, which had deceived many before, with which she wiped the feet of the Lord. She had no curling caps nor creaking little shoes nor eyes blackened with antimony — the fouler, the fairer. What place have rouge and white lead on the face of a Christian woman? Of these the one counterfeits the redness of the cheeks and lips, the other the whiteness of the face and neck: fires for young men, fuel for lusts, signs of an unchaste mind. How can she weep for her sins who lays her skin bare with tears and draws furrows in her face? That adornment is not the Lord's; that veiling is Antichrist's. With what confidence does she lift up to heaven a face that her Maker would not recognize? In vain is youth alleged and the age of girlhood asserted: a widow who has ceased to please her husband and is, according to the Apostle, truly a widow, has need of nothing but perseverance. She remembers her former pleasure, she knows what she has lost, in what she delighted: the burning arrows of the devil must be quenched with the cold of fastings and vigils. Either we must speak as we are dressed, or be dressed as we speak. Why do we promise one thing and display another? The tongue rings out chastity, and the whole body proclaims unchastity.

8. So much for what pertains to dress and adornment. As for the rest, the widow "who lives in pleasures" — it is not my word, but the Apostle's — "though living, is dead." What does this mean, that she says: "though living, is dead"? She seems indeed to be living to those who do not know, and not to be dead to sin; but to Christ, whom secret things do not deceive, she is dead. For the soul that sins shall itself die. Some men's sins are manifest, going before to judgment; but some they also follow after. In like manner also the good deeds are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot be hid. What he says is of this kind: some sin so freely and openly that, after you have seen them, you at once understand them to be sinners; but others, who cunningly conceal their vices, we recognize from their subsequent conduct. Likewise also the good are in some openly apparent, in others we learn of it by long acquaintance. Why, then, is it needful for us to boast of a chastity which, without its companions and appendages — continence and frugality — cannot make itself credible? The Apostle wears down his own body and subjects it to the command of the soul, lest he himself should not keep what he enjoins on others: and shall fervent youth, with the body fed, be secure about its chastity?

9. Nor in saying this do I condemn the foods which God created to be used with thanksgiving, but I assert that to young men and girls they are incentives to pleasures. Not the fires of Etna, not the land of Vulcan, not Vesuvius and Olympus seethe with such heat as the youthful marrow, filled with wine, inflamed with feasting. Avarice is trampled down by most, and is laid aside along with the purse; a slanderous tongue is corrected by enjoined silence; the care of the body and the fashion of dress is changed in the space of a single hour; all the other sins are external, and what is on the outside is easily cast off: lust alone, implanted by God for the procreation of children, if it has gone beyond its bounds, overflows into vice, and by a certain law of nature strains to burst forth into union. It is therefore a great virtue and one of anxious diligence to overcome what you are born in the flesh, not to live carnally, to fight with yourself daily and to watch the enclosed enemy with a hundred eyes, like Argus, as the fables tell. This is what the Apostle said in other words: Every sin that a man does is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. The physicians, and those who have written on the nature of human bodies, and especially Galen in the books entitled On Healthful Things, say that the bodies of boys and young men, and of men and women in the perfect age, glow with an implanted heat, and that to these ages those foods are harmful which increase heat, and that it conduces to health to take cool things in food and drink — just as, on the contrary, hot foods and old wines profit the old, who suffer from phlegm and cold. Hence the Saviour too says: Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life. And the Apostle: Wine, in which is luxury. Nor is it any wonder that the potter felt this about the little vessel which he himself fashioned, when even the comic poet, whose end is to know and describe human manners, said: Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.

10. First, therefore, if the firmness of your stomach allows it, take water as your drink until you pass the years of girlhood, since by nature it is most cold; or, if weakness forbids this, hear with Timothy: Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent infirmities. Then, in the foods themselves, avoid whatever is hot — I speak not only of flesh, concerning which the vessel of election gives his sentence: It is good not to drink wine and not to eat flesh — but even among the pulses themselves whatever is flatulent and heavy is to be shunned; and know that nothing so conduces to the good of young Christians as the eating of herbs, whence he also says in another place: He who is weak, let him eat herbs — and the heat of the body must be tempered with cooler fare. But if the three children and Daniel fed on pulses, they were children, and had not yet come to the frying-pan in which the king of Babylon fried the elders, the judges. We do not seek the care of the body, which in them — apart from the privilege of the grace of God — had shone forth from food of this kind, but the vigour of the soul, which is made stronger by the weakness of the flesh. Hence it is that not a few of those who aim at a chaste life collapse in the middle of the journey, while they think abstinence consists in flesh alone, and load their stomachs with pulses, which, taken moderately and sparingly, are harmless. And to say what I think: nothing so inflames the body and titillates the genital members as undigested food and disordered belching. I would rather, my daughter, that you risked your modesty for a little while than your case. Whatever is a seed-bed of pleasures, I count as poison. Let sparing food and a belly always hungry be preferred to three-day fasts, and it is far better to take a little daily than to take enough rarely. That rain is best which descends gently upon the earth; a sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields headlong.

11. When you eat, think that you must at once pray, at once read. Have a fixed number of verses from the Holy Scriptures; render this task to your Lord, and do not yield your limbs to rest before you have filled the basket of your breast with this weft. After the Holy Scriptures, read the treatises of learned men — those only whose faith is known. You have no need to seek gold in mire: with many pearls buy the one pearl. Stand with Jeremiah in the many ways, that you may come to that way which leads to the Father. Transfer the love of necklaces and gems and silken garments to the knowledge of the Scriptures. Enter the land of promise flowing with milk and honey; eat fine flour and oil; be clothed with Joseph in many-coloured garments; let your ears be pierced with Jerusalem by the word of God, that the precious grains of the new harvests may hang from them. You have the holy Exuperius, of approved age and faith, who may frequently instruct you with his admonitions.

12. Make to yourself friends of the unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into the everlasting tabernacles. Bestow your riches on those who buy not Phasian birds but common bread, who drive out hunger, who do not increase luxury. Understand the needy and the poor. Give to everyone who asks you, but most of all to those of the household of faith: clothe the naked, feed the hungry, visit the sick; as often as you stretch out your hand, think of Christ, and take care lest, while your Lord begs, you increase the riches of strangers.

13. Flee the company of young men. Let the roof of your house not look upon the long-haired, the trim, the wanton. Let the singer be driven off as harmful; banish from your dwelling the lute-girls and harp-girls and that whole choir of the devil, like the death-bringing songs of the Sirens. Do not go out again and again into public, and be carried about with the liberty of widows, an army of eunuchs going before you. It is a most wretched custom when the frail sex and the weak age abuses its own discretion and thinks that whatever pleases it is permitted. All things indeed are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let no curl-headed steward, nor handsome foster-brother, nor fair and ruddy attendant cleave to your side: sometimes the mind of mistresses is judged by the dress of their servants. Seek the society of holy virgins and widows, and, if the necessity of conversing with men presses upon you, do not avoid witnesses, and let there be such confidence in your conversation that, when another enters, you neither take fright nor blush. The face is the mirror of the mind, and the silent eyes confess the secrets of the heart. We have lately seen a scandal flit through the whole East: the age, the dress, the bearing, the gait, the indiscriminate company, the choice banquets, the royal apparel told of the nuptials of Nero and Sardanapalus. Let the wound of others be our caution; When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be the wiser.
Holy love has no impatience; a false rumour is quickly suppressed, and a later life judges of an earlier. It cannot indeed be that anyone should pass through the courses of this life without the bite of men, and it is the consolation of the worse to carp at the good, while they think the fault of sinners is lessened by the multitude of those who sin; but nevertheless the fire of the stubble quickly subsides, and the overflowing flame, its nourishment failing, gradually dies away. If last year the report lied, or, if indeed it spoke the truth, the vice has ceased, the rumour too will cease. I say this not because I fear anything sinister of you, but because, with the affection of piety, I am fearful even for what is safe. O if you could see your sister, and if it fell to you to hear in person that eloquence of her sacred mouth, you would discern great spirits in a little body, you would hear the whole furniture of the Old and New Testament glowing forth from her heart! She holds fasting for sport, prayer for delight. She holds the timbrel after the example of Miriam, and, when Pharaoh was drowned, leads the choir of virgins, singing: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; the horse and the rider he has thrown into the sea.
Such are the psaltery-girls she teaches for Christ, such the lute-girls she trains for the Saviour. So the day, so the night is spent, and, with oil prepared for the lamps, the coming of the Bridegroom is awaited. Imitate therefore your kinswoman also: let Rome have what Bethlehem, narrower than the city of Rome, possesses.

14. You have wealth; it is easy for you to supply to the needy the means of sustenance. Let virtue spend what was being prepared for luxury; let no woman who is about to despise marriage fear poverty. Redeem virgins, whom you may lead into the Saviour's chamber; receive widows, whom, like certain violets, you may mingle among the lilies of virgins and the roses of martyrs; in place of the crown of thorns, in which Christ bore the sins of the world, weave such garlands. Let that most noble man, your father, rejoice and assist; let him learn from his daughter what he had learned from his wife. Already his head is white, his knees tremble, his teeth fall out, and he furrows his unseemly brow with wrinkles; death is near at the doors, the pyre is being marked out close by: willing or unwilling, we are old men. Let him prepare for himself the provision needful for a long journey. Let him carry with him what he must leave behind unwillingly; nay rather, let him send on before him to heaven what, if he does not part with it, the earth will take.

15. Young widows are wont — some of whom have already turned back after Satan, when they have wantoned against Christ — being in heat, to say: "My little patrimony perishes daily, the inheritance of my forefathers is squandered, a servant has spoken insolently, a maid has neglected my command. Who will go out into public? Who will answer for the tributes of the fields? Who will educate my little ones? Who will rear my home-born slaves?" And — oh, the wickedness! — they set this up as the reason for marriage, the very thing that alone ought to have hindered the marriage. A mother brings in over her sons not a stepfather but an enemy, not a parent but a tyrant. Inflamed with lust, she forgets her own womb, and amid her little ones, who know not her miseries, she who was lately a new bride is decked out, mourning. Why do you allege your patrimony, why the insolence of the servants? Confess the baseness. No woman takes a husband for this, that she may not sleep with her husband. Or, if indeed lust does not goad you, what so great madness is it to prostitute chastity after the manner of harlots, that riches may be increased, and that, for a cheap and perishable thing, chastity, which is both precious and eternal, should be defiled? If you have children, why do you seek marriage? If you have none, why do you not fear the barrenness you have proved, and prefer an uncertain thing to certain modesty? The marriage-tablets are now drawn up for you, so that after a little while you may be compelled to make a will. The husband's infirmity will be feigned, and what he will wish you, who are to die, to do, he, who is to live, will himself do. Or, if it should happen that you have children by a second husband, there is domestic strife, a war within the household. It will not be permitted you to love your children, nor to look with even eyes upon those whom you have borne. You will hold out food secretly; he will envy the dead, and unless you hate your sons, you will still seem to love their father. But if, having offspring by a former wife, he has brought you into his house, even if you are most gentle, all the comedies and the mime-writers and the common topics of the rhetoricians will declaim against the most cruel stepmother. If the stepson falls ill and his head aches, you will be defamed as a poisoner. If you do not give him food, you will be called cruel; if you give it, a worker of evil. I ask you, what so great good have second marriages that they can outweigh these evils?

16. Do we wish to know what widows ought to be? Let us read the Gospel according to Luke: And there was, he says, Anna a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. Anna is interpreted "grace"; Phanuel in our tongue sounds "the face of God"; Asher is rendered either "into blessedness" or "into riches." Because, then, from her youth until eighty-four years she had borne the burden of widowhood and did not depart from the temple of God, persevering day and night in fastings and prayers, therefore she merited spiritual grace, and is called the daughter of the face of God, and is reckoned among her forefathers in blessedness and riches. Let us recall the widow of Sarepta, who preferred Elijah's hunger to her own safety and her sons', and, herself about to die that very night with her son, left her guest surviving, choosing rather to lose life than almsgiving, and in a handful of meal prepared for herself a seed-bed of the Lord's harvest. The meal is sown, and a cruse of oil springs up. In Judaea there was a scarcity of grain — for the grain of wheat had there died — and among the Gentiles streams of oil flowed for the widow. We read of Judith — if anyone, however, is willing to receive the volume — a widow worn out with fastings and squalid in mourning dress, who mourned not her dead husband but, in the squalor of her body, sought the coming of her Bridegroom. I see her hand armed with a sword, her right hand bloody; I recognize the head of Holofernes, carried back from the midst of the enemy. A woman conquers men, and chastity beheads lust; and, her dress suddenly changed, she returns to her victorious squalor, cleaner than all the adornments of the world.

17. Some, unskilfully, count Deborah too among the widows, and think the leader Barak the son of Deborah, though Scripture records otherwise. For us she shall be named for this: that she was a prophetess and is reckoned in the order of the judges. And because she could say, How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth, she received the name of "bee," fed on the flowers of the Scriptures, suffused with the fragrance of the Holy Spirit, and composing with prophetic mouth the sweet juices of ambrosia. Naomi, whose name sounds with us "comforted," whom we may interpret "the consoled," her husband and children having died abroad, brought back chastity to her native land, and, sustained by this provision, kept her Moabite daughter-in-law, that the prophecy of Isaiah might be fulfilled: Send forth a lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert. I come to the widow in the Gospel, the poor little widow, richer than all the people of Israel, who, taking a grain of mustard seed and putting leaven into the three measures of meal, tempered by the grace of the Holy Spirit the confession of the Father and the Son, and cast two mites into the treasury — whatever she could have in her substance — and offered all her riches in both Testaments of her faith. These are the two seraphim glorifying the Trinity thrice, and laid up in the treasury of the church, whence too, with the tongs of both instruments, the burning coal is taken up that purges the lips of the sinner.

18. Why should I recall ancient things and bring forth the virtues of women from books, when you can set before your eyes many in the city in which you live, whose example you ought to imitate? And, that I may not seem to run through them one by one in flattery, the holy Marcella suffices for you, who, answering to her stock, told us something from the Gospel. Anna had lived seven years with her husband after her virginity, this woman seven months; the one awaited the coming of Christ, this one holds him whom the other received; the one sang of him as he wailed in the cradle, this one proclaims him triumphant; the one spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Jerusalem, this one cries out with the redeemed nations: A brother does not redeem; a man shall redeem, and from another psalm: A man is born in her, and the Most High himself has founded her. I know that about two years ago I published books against Jovinian, in which I crushed, by the authority of the Scriptures, the questions raised on the other side, where the Apostle allows second marriages. And it is not necessary to write the same things over again, since you can borrow from there what has been written. This only, that I may not exceed the measure of a letter, I would have you admonished of: think that you are to die every day, and you will never think of a second marriage.

1. Great themes are not borne by small talents, and in the very attempt, having dared beyond their strength, they sink down; and the greater the thing to be said, the more is he overwhelmed who cannot unfold the magnitude of the matter in words. My Nepotian, yours, ours — nay, Christ's, and because he is Christ's, therefore the more ours — has left behind old men, and, wounded by the dart of longing for him, has worn them out with intolerable grief. Him whom we thought our heir, we hold as a corpse. For whom now shall my talent sweat? Whom shall my little writings be eager to please? Where is that taskmaster of ours, and the voice sweeter than the swan's song? My mind is stunned, my hand trembles, my eyes grow dim, my tongue stammers. Whatever I say, since he will not hear it, seems mute. The very pen, as if feeling it, and the wax, somewhat sadder, are overspread with rust or mould. As often as I strive to burst forth into words and to scatter the flowers of this epitaph over his tomb, so often my eyes fill, and with renewed grief I am wholly at his funeral. It was once the custom that over the bodies of the dead the children should speak their praises in the assembly from the rostra, and, like mournful songs, should rouse the breasts of the hearers to weeping and groaning: behold, the order of things is changed for us, and to our calamity Nature has lost her rights: what a young man should have rendered to old men, this we old men render to a young man.

2. What, then, shall I do? Shall I join with you in tears? But the Apostle forbids it, calling the dead among Christians "those who sleep," and the Lord in the Gospel says: The girl is not dead, but sleeps. Lazarus too, because he had slept, was raised. Shall I be glad and rejoice that he was taken away, lest wickedness should change his mind, because his soul pleased God? But against my will and resistance the tears flow down my cheeks, and amid the precepts of virtue and the hope of the resurrection the feeling of longing breaks my believing mind. O Death, who dividest brothers and, cruel and hard, severest those joined in love! The Lord brought a burning wind, rising from the desert, which dried up your veins and made desolate your fountain. You devoured Jonah indeed, but even in your belly he was alive. You bore him as though dead, that the tempest of the world might be stilled and our Nineveh be saved by his proclaiming. He, he conquered you, he slew you — that fugitive prophet who left his house and gave his beloved soul into the hands of those who sought it. He who once threatened you sternly through Hosea: I will be your death, O Death; I will be your sting, O hell — by his death you have died, by his death we live. You devoured, and you were devoured; and while you are caught by the allurement of the assumed body and think it a prey for your greedy jaws, your inward parts were pierced through with a hooked tooth.

3. We give you thanks, Christ our Saviour — we, your creature — that, while you were slain, you slew so powerful an adversary of ours. Who before was more wretched than man, who, prostrate with the eternal terror of death, had received the sense of living only for this, that he might perish? For death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression. If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were in hell, who was in the kingdom of heaven? If your friends, under the penalty of Adam's offence, and even those who had not sinned, were held liable for the sins of others, what is to be believed of those who said in their hearts, "There is no God," who became corrupt and abominable in their desires, who turned aside, and together became unprofitable; there is none that does good, no, not one? But if Lazarus is seen in Abraham's bosom and in a place of refreshment, what likeness is there between hell and the kingdom of heaven? Before Christ, Abraham among the dead; after Christ, the thief in paradise. And therefore at his resurrection many bodies of those who slept arose, and were seen in the heavenly Jerusalem. And then was fulfilled that saying: Arise, you who sleep, and lift yourself up, and Christ shall enlighten you. John the Baptist cries aloud in the desert: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. For from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. That flaming sword, the guardian of paradise, and the cherubim presiding at the gates, have been quenched and unbarred by the blood of Christ. Nor is it any wonder that this is promised to us at the resurrection, since all of us who live in the flesh but not according to the flesh have our citizenship in heaven, and to us, still placed on earth, it is said: The kingdom of God is within you.

4. Add that before the resurrection of Christ God was known only in Judaea, in Israel his name was great, and even those who knew him were nevertheless dragged down to hell. Where then were the men of the whole world, from India to Britain, from the rigid region of the north to the heats of the Atlantic ocean — so innumerable peoples and the multitudes of so many nations, as various in tongue as in dress and arms? Like fishes and locusts, like flies and gnats, they were ground down; for without the knowledge of his Creator, every man is a beast. But now the passion of Christ and his resurrection are sounded by the voices and the writings of all nations. I say nothing of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, which nations the Lord consecrated to his faith in the title of the cross. The soul immortal and subsisting after the dissolution of the body — which Pythagoras dreamed of, which Democritus did not believe, which Socrates discoursed of in prison for the consolation of his condemnation — the Indian, the Persian, the Goth, the Egyptian now philosophize about. The fierceness of the Bessi and the throng of skin-clad peoples, who once sacrificed men at the funeral rites of the dead, have broken their harsh cry into the sweet melody of the cross, and the one voice of the whole world is Christ.

5. What are we doing, O my soul? Whither do we turn? What do we take up first? What do we pass over in silence? The precepts of the rhetoricians have slipped from you, and, taken up with mourning, oppressed with tears, hindered by sobs, you do not keep the order of speaking! Where is that study of letters from infancy, and the ever-praised maxim of Anaxagoras and Telamon: "I knew that I had begotten a mortal"? We have read Crantor, whose volume Cicero followed to console his own grief; we have run through the little works of Plato, Diogenes, Clitomachus, Carneades, Posidonius, written to assuage mourning — men who in various ages, in books or letters, strove to lessen the laments of various people, so that, even if our own talent were dry, it might be watered from their fountains. They set forth innumerable men, and especially Pericles and Xenophon the Socratic, of whom the one, having lost two sons, discoursed crowned in the assembly, the other, when while sacrificing he had heard that his son was killed in war, is said to have laid down his crown and to have set it again on his head, after he found that the youth had fallen fighting bravely in the line of battle. Why should I mention the Roman generals, by whose virtues, like so many stars, the Latin histories shine? Pulvillus, while dedicating the Capitol, on hearing — so it was reported — of the sudden death of his son, ordered him to be buried in his absence; Lucius Paulus, within seven days, between the funerals of two sons, entered the city in triumph. I pass over the Maximi, the Catos, the Galli, the Pisos, the Bruti, the Scaevolae, the Metelli, the Scauri, the Marii, the Crassi, the Marcelli, and the Aufidii, whose virtue in mourning was no less than in war, and whose bereavements Tullius set forth in his book On Consolation — lest I seem to have sought what belongs to others rather than what is our own; although these things too have been briefly said to our reproach, if faith does not furnish what unbelief has shown.

6. Let us come, then, to our own. I will not lament with Jacob and David their sons who die under the Law, but with Christ in the Gospel I will receive those who rise again. The mourning of the Jews is the joy of Christians. In the evening weeping shall linger, and in the morning gladness.
The night has gone before, but the day has drawn near. Hence too Moses, dying, is mourned, while Joshua is buried on the mountain without funeral and tears. Whatever can be said from the Scriptures about lamentation, we set forth briefly in that book in which we consoled Paula at Rome. Now we must come to the same place by another path, lest we seem to tread footsteps once past and worn.

7. We know indeed that our Nepotian is with Christ and mingled among the choirs of the saints, and that what among us he searched out from afar on earth and sought by reasoning, there, seeing it close at hand, he says: As we have heard, so also we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God. But the longing for his absence we cannot bear, grieving not for his lot but for our own. The happier he is, the more are we in grief, that we lack so great a good. The sisters too wept for Lazarus, whom they knew would rise again; and, to express the true feelings of a man, the Saviour himself wept for him whom he was about to raise. His Apostle too, who had said, I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, and elsewhere, To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain, gives thanks that Epaphras was restored to him from the nearness of death, lest he should have sorrow upon sorrow — not from the fear of unbelief, but from the longing of love. How much more do you — both uncle and bishop, that is, a father in the flesh and in the spirit — long for your own heart, and sigh for it as if torn away from you! But I beseech you to set a measure to your grief, mindful of that maxim: Nothing in excess; and, your wound bound up a little, hear the praises of him whose virtue ever gladdened you, and grieve not that you have lost such a one, but rejoice that you have had such a one; and, as those who paint the regions of the earth on a small tablet, so in this little volume may you discern the marks of his virtues sketched, not fully drawn, and receive from us not strength but goodwill.

8. It is a precept of the rhetoricians that the forefathers of him who is to be praised, and their deeds, should be recalled from far back, and that the discourse should thus come to the man himself by degrees, so that, of course, he may be made more illustrious by ancestral and paternal virtues, and may seem either not to have degenerated from good men, or himself to have adorned mediocre ones. But I will not look, in praising the soul, for the goods of the flesh, which he himself always despised, nor will I boast of his birth — that is, of goods belonging to others — since both Abraham and Isaac, holy men, begot sinners, Ishmael and Esau, and, on the other hand, Jephthah, numbered in the catalogue of the just by the Apostle's voice, was born of a harlot. The soul, he says, that sins, shall itself die; therefore the soul that has not sinned shall itself live. Neither the virtues nor the vices of parents are imputed to their children; we are reckoned from the time when we are born again in Christ. Paul, the persecutor of the Church, in the morning a ravening wolf of Benjamin, in the evening gave food to Ananias, bowing his head as a sheep. Therefore let our Nepotian too, like a wailing little infant and an untaught boy, be suddenly born to us from the Jordan.

9. Another, perhaps, would write that for his salvation you left the East and the desert, and lured me, your dearest companion, with the hope of returning, that first, if it could be done, you might preserve your widowed sister with her little one, and then, if she should reject the plan, at least preserve your sweetest nephew. For this is he of whom I once prophesied to you: "Though a little nephew hang upon your neck." Another, I say, would report that in the service of the palace, beneath the cloak and the gleaming linen, his body was worn by a hair-shirt; that, standing before the powers of the world, he wore a face pale with fastings; that, still under the garments of another, he served another, and had his belt for this, that he might come to the aid of widows, orphans, the oppressed, the wretched: but these delays of an imperfect service of God do not please me, and the centurion Cornelius, whom I read to have been just, I hear at once baptized.

10. Nevertheless, let us approve, as it were, certain cradles of his nascent faith, so that he who was a devoted soldier under another's standards may be granted the laurel after he has begun to serve his own King. His belt laid aside and his dress changed, whatever there was of his military savings he distributed to the poor. For he had read: He who wishes to be perfect, let him sell all that he has and give to the poor and follow me; and again: You cannot serve two masters, God and mammon. Apart from a cheap tunic and a covering to match, which excluded the cold by merely covering the body, he reserved nothing more for himself. His very dress, following the custom of the province, was remarkable neither for elegance nor for squalor. And though he burned daily either to go to the monasteries of Egypt, or to visit the choirs of Mesopotamia, or at least to occupy the solitudes of the islands of Dalmatia, which are separated from Altinum only by a strait, he did not dare to forsake his uncle the bishop, seeing in him all the examples of the virtues, and having at home the source from which he might learn. In one and the same man he both imitated the monk and venerated the bishop. Not, as is wont to happen in most cases, did constant nearness produce familiarity, and familiarity contempt for him; but he so revered him as a parent, and so admired him as though he beheld him new each day.
Why say more? He becomes a cleric, and through the usual degrees is ordained presbyter. Good Jesus, what groans, what wailings, what refusal of food, what shunning of all eyes! Then for the first and only time he was angry with his uncle. He complained that he could not bear it, and pleaded that his youthful age was unsuited to the priesthood. But the more he resisted, the more he stirred up the zeal of all toward himself, and merited by refusing what he did not wish to be, and was the worthier for crying out that he was unworthy. We saw a Timothy of our own time, and gray hairs in wisdom, and a man chosen presbyter by Moses, whom Moses himself knew to be a presbyter. Therefore, understanding the clergy not as an honour but a burden, he made it his first care to overcome envy by humility, and then to give no tale of shameful rumour against himself, so that those who carped at his age might be astonished at his continence. To come to the aid of the poor, to visit the sick, to invite to hospitality, to soothe with kindness, to rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep; he was the staff of the blind, the food of the hungry, the hope of the wretched, the solace of the mourning. Thus he was eminent in each single virtue, as though he had none of the rest. Among the presbyters and his equals, first in work, last in rank. Whatever good he had done, he ascribed to his uncle; if anything by chance had turned out otherwise than he thought, he said that his uncle did not know of it and that he himself had erred. In public he knew him as bishop, at home as father. He tempered the gravity of his manners with cheerfulness of countenance. You would understand his joy by a smile, not by loud laughter. He honoured the widows and virgins of Christ as mothers, and exhorted them as sisters, with all chastity. Now, after he had betaken himself home, and, leaving the cleric outside, had given himself to the hardness of the monks, frequent in prayers, watchful in supplication, he offered his tears to God, not to men; he moderated his fastings, charioteer-like, according to the weariness and strength of his body. He attended his uncle's table, and so tasted whatever was set before him that he both shunned superstition and preserved continence. His conversation, and every meal, was to propose something from the Scriptures, to listen gladly, to answer modestly, to take up what was right, not sharply to refute what was wrong, to instruct rather than to vanquish one disputing against him, and, with an ingenuous modesty that adorned his age, to confess simply whose each saying was; and in this way, by declining the glory of learning, he was held most learned. "That," he would say, "is Tertullian's, this Cyprian's, this Lactantius's, that Hilary's. So spoke Minucius Felix, so Victorinus, in this manner Arnobius." Me too, because he loved me for his uncle's fellowship, he sometimes brought forward into the open. By constant reading too and long meditation he had made his breast a library of Christ.

11. How often did he beg, in letters from across the sea, that I would write something to him!
