How often did he set before me the nocturnal petitioner of the Gospel, and the widow who importuned the harsh judge! And when I refused by silence rather than by letters, and put the modesty of one keeping silent to the blush of the one asking, he set up against me his uncle as a pleader, who might both ask more freely on another's behalf and obtain more easily out of reverence for his priesthood. I did, then, what he wished, and in a little book consecrated our friendship to eternal memory; on receiving which he boasted that he had surpassed the wealth of Croesus and the riches of Darius. He held it with his eyes, in his bosom, in his hands, in his mouth; and while he often unrolled it in his bed, the sweet page fell upon the breast of the sleeper. But if any of the strangers or friends came, he rejoiced over himself at my testimony, and whatever was lacking in the little work he made up by measured pauses and variety of delivery, so that in his reciting it he himself seemed daily either to please or to displease. Whence this fervour, save from the love of God? Whence the untiring meditation on the law of Christ, save from longing for him who gave the law? Let others add coin to coin and, choking their purse, hunt the wealth of matrons by their attentions; let them be richer monks than they had been worldlings, possessing under a poor Christ the wealth they had not had under a wealthy devil, and let the Church sigh over them as rich whom the world held beggars before: our Nepotian, trampling on gold, pursues sheets of writing; but, as he is a despiser of himself in the flesh and walks the more adorned for his poverty, so he searches out all the adornment of the Church.

12. In comparison indeed with what was said above, the things we are about to say are slight, but even in small things the same spirit is shown. For just as we admire the Creator not only in heaven and earth, in the sun and ocean, in elephants, camels, horses, oxen, leopards, bears, lions, but also in the tiniest animals — the ant, the gnat, flies, little worms, and that kind of creature whose bodies we know better than their names — and venerate the same skill in all, so the mind devoted to Christ is equally intent on greater things and on lesser, knowing that an account must be rendered even for an idle word. He was anxious, therefore, whether the altar gleamed, whether the walls were free of soot, whether the floors were wiped clean, whether there was a doorkeeper frequent at the gate, the curtains always at the doorways, whether the sanctuary was clean, the vessels shining; and his pious solicitude, disposed over all the ceremonies, neglected no duty, lesser or greater. Wherever in the church you sought him, you would find him.
Antiquity admires the noble man Quintus Fabius, who is also a writer of Roman history, but who got his name more from painting than from letters; and Scripture testifies that our Bezalel was full of wisdom and the spirit of God, and Hiram too, the son of a Tyrian woman, in that the one fashioned the furniture of the tabernacle, the other of the temple. For just as glad crops and rich fields sometimes luxuriate in stalks and ears, so distinguished talents and a mind full of virtues overflow into the elegance of various arts. Hence among the Greeks that philosopher is praised who boasted that everything he used, even to his cloak and ring, was made by his own hand. This same thing we can say of him too, who would overshade the basilicas of the church and the chapels of the martyrs with various flowers and the foliage of trees and the tendrils of vines, so that whatever pleased in the church, both in arrangement and in appearance, bore witness to the labour and zeal of the presbyter.

13. Well done, in virtue. Of one whose beginnings are such, what will the end be? O wretched human condition, and vain is all our living without Christ. Why do you withdraw, why do you turn aside, O speech? For as though we could put off his death and make his life longer, so we fear to come to the end. All flesh is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. Where now is that comely face, where the dignity of the whole body, with which, as with a beautiful garment, the beauty of the soul was clothed? It withered, alas, as the lily under the blowing south wind, and the purple of the violet gradually passed into pallor. And when he burned with fevers and the heat drained the fountains of his veins, with weary breath he consoled his sorrowing uncle. His face was glad, and while all around were weeping, he alone smiled. To cast off his cloak, to stretch out his hands, to see what others did not see, and, as if rising to meet them, to greet those who came: you would understand that he was not dying but migrating, and changing his friends, not leaving them. The tears roll down my face, and with hardened mind I cannot disguise the grief I suffer. Who would believe that at such a time he remembered our intimacy, and that, with his soul struggling, he knew the sweetness of our studies? Taking his uncle's hand: "This tunic," he said, "which I used in the ministry of Christ, send to him who is most beloved by me, in age my father, in fellowship my brother, and whatever of affection was owed by you to your nephew, transfer it to him whom you loved equally with me." And with such words he failed, holding his uncle by the hand, touching me in remembrance.

14. I know that you would not have wished thus to prove the love of your fellow-citizens toward you, and that you would rather have sought the affection of your country in prosperity. But a duty of this kind is more pleasant in good fortune, more welcome in ill. The whole city mourned him, all Italy mourned him. The earth received his body, his soul was rendered to Christ. You sought a nephew, the Church a priest. Your successor has gone before you. What you were, he, after you, deserved to be by the judgment of all. And so from one house a double dignity of the episcopate came forth: while in the one there is congratulation that he held it, in the other grief that he was snatched away, that he might not hold it. It is the maxim of Plato that all the life of the wise man is a meditation upon death. The philosophers praise this and bear it to the skies, but far more strongly the Apostle: I die daily, he says, by your glory. It is one thing to attempt, another to do; one thing to live as one about to die, another to die as one about to live. The former is to die from glory; the latter dies ever toward glory.
We too, therefore, ought to premeditate in our minds that one day we shall be what — willing or unwilling — cannot be far off. For if we exceeded nine hundred years of life, as the human race lived before the flood, and the times of Methuselah were granted us, yet the past length would be nothing, since it would have ceased to be. For between him who lived ten years and him who lived a thousand, after the same end of life has come and the unrefusable necessity of death, all that has passed is just as much — except that the older man sets out the more laden with the burden of his sins.
For wretched mortals, the best day of life flies first; diseases come on, and sad old age, and toil, and the harshness of unrelenting death snatches them away.
The poet Naevius says: A mortal must of necessity suffer many ills. Hence antiquity feigned that Niobe, who wept much, was turned into stone, and others into various beasts, and Hecuba into a dog; and Hesiod, lamenting the births of men, rejoices at their funerals; and Ennius prudently says:
The common people, he says, in this surpass the king's estate: the people may weep, the king honourably may not.
As with a king, so with a bishop — nay, less with a king than with a bishop. For the king rules over the unwilling, the bishop over the willing; the one subjects by terror, the other lords it by service; the one guards bodies unto death, the other preserves souls unto life. Upon you the eyes of all are turned; your house and conduct, set as it were on a watchtower, are the mistress of public discipline. Whatever you do, all think they must do for themselves. Take care that you commit nothing which either those who wish to find fault may seem worthily to have torn apart, or those who wish to imitate you may be compelled to transgress. Conquer as far as you can — nay, more than you can — the softness of your mind, and check the abundantly flowing tears, lest a great affection for a nephew be reckoned, among unbelieving minds, as despair toward God. He is to be longed for by you as one absent, not as one dead, so that you may seem to await him, not to have lost him.

15. But what am I doing, healing a grief which I think is already assuaged both by time and by reason, instead of rather setting before you the recent miseries of kings and the calamities of our own time, so that he who has been deprived of this light is not so much to be mourned as to be congratulated, that he has escaped from such great evils? Constantius, the patron of the Arian heresy, while preparing against an enemy and being borne in haste to battle, dying in the little village of Mopsus, left the empire, to his great grief, to his foe. Julian, the destroyer of his own soul and the butcher of a Christian army, felt Christ in Media, whom he had first denied in Gaul; and while he wished to extend the bounds of the Romans, he lost those already extended. Jovian, having only tasted the goods of royalty, perished, suffocated by the fumes of coals, showing all what human power is. Valentinian, his native soil laid waste and his country left unavenged, was extinguished by a vomiting of blood. His brother Valens, conquered in the Gothic war in Thrace, had there the same place for his death and his sepulchre. Gratian, betrayed by his own army and not received by the cities he came to, was a mockery to his enemy, and the walls of your city, Lyons, bear witness to the traces of the bloody hand. The young Valentinian, almost a boy, after flight, after exile, after recovering the empire with much blood, was slain not far from the city, the conscious witness of his brother's death, and his lifeless corpse was dishonoured by hanging. What shall I say of Procopius, Maximus, Eugenius, who certainly, while they held power, were a terror to nations? All stood captive before the faces of their conquerors, and — what is most wretched for those once most powerful — were pierced first by the ignominy of slavery before the enemy's sword.

16. Someone may say: "Such is the condition of kings, and lightnings strike the highest mountains." Let me come to private dignities, and I will not speak of those who do not last two years; and, to pass over the rest, it is enough for us to write of the various ends of three recent consulars. Abundantius, in need, is in exile at Pityus; the head of Rufinus was carried on a pike to Constantinople, and his severed right hand, to the disgrace of his insatiable avarice, begged alms from door to door; Timasius, cast down suddenly from the highest step of dignity, thinks himself to have escaped because he lives, inglorious, at Assa. I tell not the calamities of the wretched but the frail state of the human condition — my mind shudders to follow the ruins of our times. It is twenty years and more that between Constantinople and the Julian Alps Roman blood is daily shed. Scythia, Thrace, Macedonia, Thessaly, Dardania, Dacia, Epirus, Dalmatia, and all the Pannonias the Goth, the Sarmatian, the Quadian, the Alan, the Huns, the Vandals, the Marcomanni lay waste, drag off, and plunder. How many matrons, how many virgins of God, and free and noble bodies, have been a sport to these beasts! Bishops taken captive, presbyters slain and clerics of various offices, churches overthrown, horses stabled at the altars of Christ, the relics of martyrs dug up: everywhere mourning, everywhere groaning, and the image of death on every side. The Roman world is falling, and yet our neck, held erect, is not bent. What spirit do you think the Corinthians now have, the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians, the Arcadians, and all Greece, over whom the barbarians rule? And indeed I have named but a few cities, in which there were once no small kingdoms. The East seemed exempt from these evils, and was only dismayed by the reports: behold, last year, from the farthest cliffs of the Caucasus, there were let loose upon us not the wolves of Arabia, but of the north, who in a short time overran so many provinces. How many monasteries were taken, how many waters of rivers were changed by human blood! Antioch was besieged, and the rest of the cities past which flow the Halys, the Cydnus, the Orontes, and the Euphrates. Flocks of captives were dragged off; Arabia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Egypt were captives in their fear.
"Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron,
could I run through all the names of the punishments."
For I have not proposed to write a history, but briefly to weep our own miseries. Otherwise, to set forth these things worthily, even Thucydides and Sallust are mute.

17. Happy Nepotian, who does not see these things; happy, who does not hear them. Wretched we, who either suffer them, or, suffering, behold our brethren in such great sufferings; and yet we wish to live, and we think those who lack these things rather to be wept for than blessed. We feel God offended long since, and we do not appease him. By our sins the barbarians are strong, by our vices the Roman army is overcome; and, as if this were not enough for disasters, civil wars have consumed almost more than the enemy's sword. Wretched the Israelites, in comparison with whom Nebuchadnezzar is called the servant of God; unhappy we, who so displease God that through the fury of the barbarians his anger rages against us. Hezekiah did penance, and a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians were destroyed by one angel in one night; Jehoshaphat sang praises in concert to the Lord, and the Lord conquered for him as he praised; Moses fought against Amalek not with the sword but with prayer. If we wish to be lifted up, let us be cast down. For shame, and the mind stupid even to unbelief! The Roman army, conqueror and lord of the world, is conquered by these men, dreads these men, is terrified at the sight of these men, who cannot walk, who, if they touch the ground, think themselves dead; and we do not understand the words of the prophets: A thousand shall flee, one pursuing; nor do we cut off the causes of the disease, that the disease may likewise be taken away, and at once behold the arrows yielding to the javelins, the tiaras to the helmets, the nags to the war-horses.

18. We have exceeded the measure of consoling, and, while we forbid the mourning of one man's death, we have lamented the dead of the whole world. Xerxes, that most powerful king, who overturned mountains and bridged seas, when from a lofty place he had beheld an infinite multitude of men and an innumerable army, is said to have wept, because after a hundred years none of those whom he then beheld would survive. O if we could climb to such a watchtower, from which we might behold the whole earth beneath our feet! Then I would show you the ruins of the whole world, nations dashed against nations and kingdoms against kingdoms; some tortured, some slain, some overwhelmed by the waves, some dragged into slavery; here a wedding, there a wailing; some being born, others dying; some flowing with riches, others begging; and not the army of Xerxes only, but the men of the whole world, who now live, soon to be gone in a brief space. Speech is overcome by the magnitude of the matter, and all that we say is too little.

19. Let us return, then, to ourselves, and, as it were descending from heaven, let us for a little while look upon our own affairs. Do you perceive, I beg you, when you became an infant, when a boy, when a youth, when of robust age, when an old man? Daily we die, daily we are changed, and yet we believe ourselves to be eternal. This very thing that I dictate, that is written, that I read over, that I correct, is drawn from my life. As many as are the points of the scribe's pen, so many are the losses of my days. We write and write back, the letters cross the seas, and, as the keel cleaves its trusting furrows through every wave, the moments of our age are diminished. We have only this gain, that we are joined to one another by the love of Christ. Charity is patient, is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; charity never fails. This always lives in the breast; through this our Nepotian, absent, is present, and embraces with both hands those divided by such great spaces of earth. We have a pledge of mutual love. Let us be joined in spirit, bound in affection, and let us imitate in his son the fortitude of mind which the blessed pope Chromatius showed at the death of his brother. Let our little page sing of him, let all our letters sound of him. Whom we cannot hold in body, let us hold in remembrance, and of him with whom we cannot speak, let us never cease to speak.

1. Nothing is happier than the Christian, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing more toilsome, who daily is in peril of his life. Nothing is stronger than he who conquers the devil; nothing weaker than he who is overcome by the flesh. Of both these things there are very many examples. The thief believed on the cross, and at once deserved to hear: Amen, amen I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise. Judas slips from the height of the apostolate into the hell of betrayal, and is broken neither by the intimacy of the meal nor by the dipping of the morsel nor by the grace of the kiss, so as not to betray as a man one whom he had known to be the Son of God. What is cheaper than the Samaritan woman? Not only did she herself believe, and after six husbands find one Lord, and recognize the Messiah at the well whom the people of the Jews in their temple knew not, but she becomes the author of the salvation of many, and, while the apostles were buying food, she refreshes the hungry one and sustains the weary one. What is wiser than Solomon? And yet he is befooled by the loves of women. Salt is good, and no sacrifice is received without its sprinkling — whence the Apostle too commands: Let your speech be seasoned with salt — but if it lose its savour, it is cast out, and so loses the dignity of its name that it is not useful even on the dunghill, with which the fields of believers are wont to be enriched and the barren soil of souls to be fattened. We say these things, that at the very first we may teach you, my son Rusticus, that you have begun great things, are pursuing lofty ones, and, trampling on the incentives of youth — nay, of puberty — are climbing a step indeed of the perfect age; but the road by which you enter is slippery, and the glory after victory is not so great as the disgrace after a fall.

2. You are not now to be led by me through the meadows of the virtues, nor must I labour to show you the beauty of the various flowers, what the lilies have of purity in them, what the modesty of roses possesses, what the purple of the violet promises in the kingdom, what the painting of glowing gems pledges. For already, the Lord being favourable, you hold the plough-handle; already you have climbed to the roof and the upper room with the apostle Peter, who, hungering among the Jews, is filled with the faith of Cornelius, and quenches the hunger of their unbelief by the conversion of the Gentiles, and in the four-cornered vessel of the gospels, which came down from heaven to the earth, is taught and learns that all men can be saved. And again, what he had seen, in the likeness of a most white sheet, is carried up to the heights, and snatches the crowds of believers from the earth to heaven, that the promise of the Lord may be fulfilled: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. The whole of what, having taken your hand, I desire to instil into you — what, like a skilled sailor after many shipwrecks, I try to teach an untrained passenger — is this: that you may know on what shore the pirate of chastity lies, where is Charybdis and the root of all evils, avarice, where are the Scyllan dogs of detractors, of whom the Apostle speaks: Lest, biting one another, you be consumed one of another; how, in the midst of calm, we may, secure, be sometimes overwhelmed by the Libyan Syrtes of the vices, and what venomous living creatures the desert of this world nourishes.

3. Those sailing the Red Sea — in which it is to be wished for us that the true Pharaoh be drowned with his army — come with many difficulties and dangers to the city of Auxuma. On either shore dwell wandering nations — nay, most ferocious beasts. Always anxious, always armed, they carry the provisions of a whole year. All things are full of hidden rocks and most dangerous shoals, so that a lookout and pilot sits at the very top of the mast and from there proclaims his orders for steering and turning the ship. The voyage is happy if after six months they reach the harbour of the aforesaid city, from which the ocean begins to open out, through which scarcely in a whole year one comes to India and to the river Ganges — which Holy Scripture calls Phison — which encircles all the land of Havilah and is said to carry forth many kinds of spices from the fountain of paradise. There is born the carbuncle and the emerald and the gleaming pearls and the unions, with which the ambition of noble women burns, and the golden mountains, which it is impossible for men to approach because of the dragons and griffins and the monsters of immense bodies, that it may be shown us what guardians avarice has.

4. To what end these things? It is clear. If the merchants of the world endure so much to come to uncertain and perishable riches, and keep at the risk of their life what they have sought with many dangers, what is not to be done by the merchant of Christ, who, having sold all things, seeks the most precious pearl, who with all the resources of his substance buys the field in which he may find the treasure that neither thief can dig up nor robber carry off?

5. I know that I shall offend very many, who refer a general discussion of the vices to their own reproach, and, while they are angry with me, reveal their own conscience, and judge much worse of themselves than of me. For I will name no one, nor, with the license of the old comedy, will I choose out and brand definite persons. It is the part of a prudent man and of prudent women to dissemble — nay, to amend — what they understand in themselves, and to be indignant with themselves rather than with me, and not to heap curses on the admonisher, who, even if he be held by the same crimes, is certainly better in this, that his own evils do not please him.

6. I hear that you have a religious mother, a widow of many years, who nourished you, who instructed you as an infant, and after the studies of the Gauls, which are of the most flourishing, sent you to Rome, not sparing expense, and bearing the absence of her son in the hope of the future, that Roman gravity might season the richness and brilliance of Gallic speech, and use upon you not spurs but reins — as we read also of the most eloquent men of Greece, who dried the Asian swelling with Attic salt, and pruned back the luxuriant vines with sickles, that the wine-presses of eloquence might overflow not with the foliage of words, but with the squeezings, as it were, of the grapes of meaning. Receive her as a parent, love her as a nurse, venerate her as holy. Nor imitate the example of others, who leave their own and seek the women of strangers, whose disgrace is in the open, seeking suspect companionships under the names of piety. I myself have known some, now of riper age and most of freedman stock, to delight in young men and seek spiritual sons, and, modesty being gradually overcome, to burst out under the feigned names of mothers into a marital license. Others forsake their virgin sisters and are coupled with strange widows. There are women who hate their own and are fondled by affection for those not their own, whose impatience, the index of the mind, admits no excuse and tears apart the empty veils of unchastity like spiders' webs. You may see not a few, with girded loins, in a dark tunic, with a long beard, unable to depart from women, dwelling under the same roof, going to banquets together, having young maids in their service, and, except for the name of marriage, all that belongs to marriage. Nor is it the fault of the Christian name if a feigner of religion be in vice; nay rather, it is the confusion of the heathen, when they see that those things displease the churches which do not please all good men.

7. But you, if you wish to be a monk and not to seem one, have care not of your household estate, which by renouncing you began to be this, but of your soul. Let the squalor of your garments be a sign of a white mind, let a cheap tunic prove your contempt of the world — provided only that the mind does not swell, that the dress and the speech do not disagree. Do not seek the warmth of the baths, you who desire to extinguish the heat of the body by the cold of fastings. Let these too be moderate, lest by their excess they weaken the stomach and, demanding a greater refreshment, break out into indigestion, which is the parent of lusts. Modest and temperate food is useful both to the flesh and to the soul. See your mother in such a way that you are not compelled through her to see others, whose faces may cling to your heart, And the silent wound lives beneath the breast. Know that the little maids who are in her service are a snare to you, because, the cheaper their condition, the easier the fall. John the Baptist too had a holy mother and was a pontiff's son, and yet he was not overcome either by his mother's affection or by his father's wealth, so as to live in his parents' house with peril to his chastity. He lived in the desert, and with eyes longing for Christ deigned to look upon nothing else. A rough garment, a leathern belt, food of locusts and wild honey, all things prepared for virtue and continence. The sons of the prophets — whom we read in the Old Testament as monks — built themselves little huts by the streams of the Jordan, and, the crowds of the cities left behind, lived on barley-meal and wild herbs. As long as you are in your own country, have your cell for a paradise; pluck the various fruits of the Scriptures, use these delights, enjoy their embrace. If your eye, your foot, your hand offend you, cast them off. Spare no one, that you may spare your soul alone. Whoever shall look upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Who shall glory that he has a chaste heart? The stars are not clean in the sight of the Lord: how much less men, whose life is a temptation! Woe to us, who, as often as we lust, so often we fornicate. My sword, he says, is drunk in heaven: how much more on the earth, which brings forth thorns and thistles. The vessel of election, in whose mouth Christ sounded, wears down his body and subjects it to servitude, and yet perceives the natural ardour of the flesh to fight against his own resolve, so that he is compelled to do what he does not wish, and, as if suffering violence, he cries out and says: Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? And do you reckon that you can pass without a fall and a wound, unless with all custody you keep your heart and say with the Saviour: My mother and my brethren are these, who do the will of my Father? That cruelty is piety; nay, what is so pious as for a holy son to guard a holy mother? She too wishes that you should live, not that she should see you for a time, that she may see you always with Christ. Anna begot Samuel not for herself, but for the tabernacle.
The sons of Jonadab, who drank no wine or strong drink, who dwelt in tents and had for their seats wherever night had compelled them, are written in the psalm to have first endured captivity, because, when the army of the Chaldeans was laying Judaea waste, they were compelled to enter the cities.

8. Let others see what they think — for each is led by his own opinion — to me a town is a prison and solitude a paradise. Why do we desire the throng of cities, we who are reckoned by our singleness? Moses, that he might be set over the people of the Jews, is trained forty years in the desert; a shepherd of sheep, he became a shepherd of men; the apostles passed from the fishing of the lake of Gennesaret to the fishing of men. Then they had a father, a net, a little boat: following the Lord, they at once left all things, daily carrying their cross and not even having a staff in their hand. This I say, that, even if the desire of the clergy tickles you, you may learn what you can teach, and offer a reasonable sacrifice to Christ, lest you be a soldier before a recruit, lest you be a master before a disciple. It is not the part of my humility nor of my measure to judge of others, and to say anything sinister of the ministers of the churches. Let them have their order and their grade; if you should hold it, how you must live in it, the book published to Nepotian can teach you. Now we are examining the cradle and manners of the monk — and of that monk who, instructed in the liberal studies, in his youth laid the yoke of Christ on his neck.

9. And first it must be treated whether you ought to live in a monastery alone or with others. To me it seems best that you should have the companionship of holy men, and not teach yourself and enter without a guide on a way you have never entered, and at once have to turn aside to the one side or the other and lie open to error, and walk either more or less than is needful — so that, running, you tire yourself, or, delaying, you fall asleep. In solitude pride quickly creeps up, and, if a man has fasted a little while and has not seen another, he thinks himself to be of some importance, and, forgetful of himself, of whence and whither he has come, within in body, in tongue he wanders abroad. He judges, against the Apostle's will, the servants of another; what gluttony demands, he stretches out his hands for; he sleeps as much as he wishes; he reveres no one, thinks all beneath himself, and is more often in the cities than in his cell, and among the brethren feigns modesty, who is jostled in the crowds of the streets. What then? Do we reprehend the solitary life? By no means, since we have often praised it. But we wish soldiers of this kind to go forth from the training-school of the monasteries: men whom the rudiments do not hold back, who have given a sample of their conduct over a long time, who have been the least of all, that they might become the first of all, whom neither hunger nor satiety ever overcame, who rejoice in poverty, whose dress, speech, countenance, gait is a teaching of the virtues, who do not know how, according to certain foolish men, to fashion portents of demons assailing them, that among the unskilled and the men of the crowd they may make a marvel of themselves and thereupon pursue gains.

10. We have lately seen, and lamented, the wealth of a Croesus caught out by one man's death, and the alms of a city, gathered as though for the uses of the poor, left behind to his stock and posterity. Then the iron, which lay hidden in the deep, floated upon the water, and amid the palm-trees of Marah the bitterness was shown. Nor is it any wonder: such a companion and master too he had, who made the hunger of the needy his own riches, and held to his own misery what was left to the wretched. Whose cry at last reached heaven and overcame the most patient ears of God, so that an angel sent said to that most wicked Nabal of Carmel: Fool, this night they shall take away your soul from you; but what you have prepared, whose shall it be?

11. I wish, therefore, both for the causes I set forth above, that you should not dwell with your mother, and especially lest, by refusing the dainty foods she offers, you sadden her, or, if you accept them, add oil to the fire, and, amid the throng of girls, see by day what you may think of by night. Let the book never depart from your hand and your eyes; let the psalter be learned word for word; let prayer be without intermission, the sense watchful and lying open to no vain thoughts. Let the body and the mind alike be stretched toward the Lord. Conquer anger by patience; love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Nor let your mind be at leisure for various perturbations, which, if they settle in the breast, will lord it over you and lead you down to the greatest offence. Do also some work, that the devil may always find you occupied. If the apostles, having the power to live by the gospel, laboured with their hands, lest they should burden anyone, and gave refreshment to others, of whom they ought to reap carnal things for spiritual, why do you not prepare what will go to your own uses? Either weave a basket of rushes or plait a hamper of pliant osiers; let the ground be dug, let the little beds be divided by an even boundary; in which, when the seeds of herbs have been cast or the plants set in order, let irrigating waters be led, that you may stand by as a spectator of most beautiful verses:
Behold, from the brow of the sloping path he draws the water, and it, falling, stirs a hoarse murmur over the smooth stones, and tempers the parched fields with its bubblings.
Let unfruitful trees be grafted, whether with buds or with shoots, and after a little while you may pluck the sweet fruits of your labour. Construct hives for bees, to which the Proverbs send you, and learn the order of the monasteries and the royal discipline in little bodies. Let nets too be woven for catching fish; let books be written, that the hand may both work for food and the soul be filled with reading. Every idle man is in desires. The monasteries of the Egyptians keep this custom, that they receive no one without work and labour, not so much for the necessities of sustenance as for the salvation of the soul, lest it should wander in pernicious thoughts and, after the manner of fornicating Jerusalem, spread its feet to everyone who passes by.

12. While I was a young man, and the deserts of solitude walled me in, I could not bear the incentives of the vices and the ardour of nature; which, though I broke with frequent fastings, yet my mind seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I gave myself for training to a certain brother who had believed from among the Hebrews, so that, after the subtleties of Quintilian and the rivers of Cicero and the gravity of Fronto and the smoothness of Pliny, I should learn an alphabet and meditate on hissing and panting words. What labour I spent there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired and how often I ceased and again began in my contention to learn, my own conscience, who suffered it, is witness, as is that of those who led their life with me. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I gather sweet fruits.

13. I will tell another thing too, which I saw in Egypt. There was a Greek young man in a monastery who by no greatness of continence, by no greatness of work, could extinguish the flame of the flesh. The father of the monastery saved him, when in this peril, by this device. He commands a certain grave man to pursue the man with quarrels and abuse, and, after the injury had been inflicted, to come first to the complaints. The witnesses, when called, spoke for him who had done the insult. He wept against the lie; no one else believed the truth; the father alone cunningly set up his defence, lest the brother should be swallowed up by an excessive sadness. Why say more? Thus a year was passed, at the end of which the young man, being asked about his former thoughts, whether he still endured any trouble, said: "Good heavens, one is not allowed to live, and one wishes to fornicate?" If he had been alone, by what helper would he have overcome?

14. The philosophers of the world are wont to drive out an old love with a new love, as a nail with a nail. This too the seven princes of the Persians did to Ahasuerus, that they might restrain his longing for Queen Vashti by the love of other girls. They remedy a vice with a vice and a sin with a sin; let us overcome vices with the love of the virtues. Decline, he says, from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. Unless we hate evil, we cannot love good. Nay rather, good must be done, that we may decline from evil; peace must be sought, that we may flee wars. Nor is it enough to seek it, unless, when found and fleeing, we pursue it with all zeal — that peace which surpasses all understanding, in which is the dwelling of God, as the prophet says: And his place was made in peace; and the pursuit of peace is beautifully named, according to that saying of the Apostle: Pursuing hospitality — so that we may invite guests not with a light and hasty word and, so to speak, with the tips of the lips, but hold them with all the ardour of the mind, as though they carried away with them something of our gain and profit.

15. No art is learned without a master. Even dumb animals and the herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees there are chiefs; the cranes follow one in a lettered order. There is one emperor, one judge of a province. Rome, as it was founded, could not have two brothers at once as kings, and is dedicated by parricide. In the womb of Rebecca, Esau and Jacob waged wars. There are single bishops of the churches, single archpresbyters, single archdeacons, and the whole ecclesiastical order rests upon its own rulers. In a ship there is one helmsman, in a house one master; in however great an army the signal of one is awaited. And, that I may not make the reader loathe me by repeating more, through all these things my discourse tends to this: to teach you that you are not to be let go at your own discretion, but ought to live in a monastery under the discipline of one father and in the company of many, that from one you may learn humility, from another patience, that this one may teach you silence, that one gentleness; that you may not do what you wish, may eat what you are bidden, may have as much as you have received, may be clothed in what you have received, may pay the tasks of your work, may be subject to one to whom you do not wish, may come weary to your bed and sleep while walking, may be compelled to rise before sleep is finished, may say a psalm in your turn — in which not the sweetness of the voice but the affection of the mind is sought, as the Apostle writes: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind; and: Singing in your hearts; for he had read that it was commanded: Sing psalms wisely — may serve the brethren, may wash the feet of guests, may keep silence when you have suffered an injury, may fear the superior of the monastery as a lord, love him as a parent, may believe that whatever he has commanded is salutary for you, and may not judge of the sentence of your elder, whose duty it is to obey and to fulfil what is commanded, as Moses says: Hear, O Israel, and be silent. Occupied with so great affairs, you will be at leisure for no thoughts; and, while you pass from one thing to another and work succeeds work, you will retain in mind that alone which you are compelled to do.

16. I myself have seen some who, after they renounced the world — in their garments only and in the profession of the voice, not in their possessions — changed nothing of their former conduct. Their household estate was rather increased than diminished; the same services of servants, the same apparatus of the banquet; in glass and an earthen dish gold is eaten, and amid the crowds and swarms of their ministers they claim for themselves the name of solitaries. But those who are poor and of slender little substance, and seem to themselves clever, proceed into public like the floats of processions, that they may exercise a canine eloquence. Others, with shoulders raised on high and croaking I know not what within themselves, with eyes fixed dully on the ground, weigh out swelling words, so that, if you added a herald, you would think the prefecture was advancing. There are those who, from the dampness of their cells and immoderate fastings, the weariness of solitude and excessive reading, while day and night they din in their own ears, are turned to madness and need the remedies of Hippocrates more than our admonitions. Very many cannot do without their former arts and trades, and, their names of traders changed, ply the same commerce, seeking not food and clothing, which the Apostle commands, but greater profits than men of the world. And formerly indeed the rage of sellers was restrained by the aediles, whom the Greeks call agoranomoi, nor was the sin unpunished; but now, under the title of religion, unjust gains are exercised, and the honour of the Christian name makes fraud rather than suffers it. And — which it is shameful to say, but necessary, that at least thus we may blush at our disgrace — publicly stretching out our hands in rags, we hide gold, and, against the opinion of all, we die rich, with full purses, we who lived as though poor. For you, when you are in a monastery, it will not be permitted to do these things; and, the custom gradually growing strong, you will begin to wish what at first you were compelled to do, and your labour will delight you, and, forgetful of the past, you will always pursue the things that are before, by no means considering what evil others do, but what good you ought to do.

17. Nor indeed be led by the multitude of those who sin, nor be made anxious by the throng of those who perish, so that you silently think: "What? Shall all then perish who dwell in the cities? Behold, they enjoy their own possessions, they minister to the churches, they go to the baths, they do not scorn ointments, and yet they live in the flower of all things." To which I have answered before, and now will answer briefly: that in the present little work I am not disputing about clerics, but instructing a monk. The clerics are holy, and the life of all of them is praiseworthy. So, then, act and live in a monastery that you may deserve to be a cleric, that you may stain your youth with no defilement, that you may proceed to the altar of Christ as a virgin from the bridal-chamber, and may have a good testimony from those outside, and that women may know your name and not know your face. When you come to the perfect age, if only life be your companion, and either the people or the bishop of the city should choose you into the clergy, do the things that are the clerics', and among them follow the better ones, because in every condition and grade the worst are mixed with the best.

18. Do not leap quickly to writing, and be led by a light madness. Learn for a long time what you may teach. Do not believe your praisers — nay, do not gladly lend your ear to mockers, who, when they have warmed you with flatteries and in a manner made you bereft of mind, if you suddenly look back, you may catch either the necks of storks bent behind you, or an ass's little ears agitated by the hand, or a dog's panting tongue stretched out. Disparage no one, nor think yourself holy if you tear others to pieces. We often accuse what we ourselves do, and, eloquent against ourselves, inveigh against our own vices, judging mute about the eloquent. Grunnius used to advance to speak with a tortoise's gait, and at certain intervals scarcely got out a few words, so that you would think him hiccuping, not speaking out. And yet, when, the table being set, he had laid out a heap of books, with eyebrow drawn up, nostrils contracted, and brow wrinkled, he snapped with two little fingers, by this sign provoking the disciples to listen. Then to pour out sheer trifles and to declaim against individuals; you would say Longinus the critic was there, and the censor of Roman eloquence noting whom he wished and excluding him from the senate of the learned. This man, well-moneyed, was the more pleasing at dinners. Nor is it any wonder, who was wont to bait many, and, a wedge formed of garrulous men clamouring around him, advanced into public, within a Nero, without a Cato, wholly ambiguous, so that out of contrary and diverse natures you would say one monster and a new beast had been compacted, according to that poetic verse:
A lion in front, a dragon behind, the very middle a chimera.

19. Never, therefore, may you see such men, nor attach yourself to men of this kind, lest you incline your heart to words of malice and hear: Sitting, you disparaged your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling-block; and again: The sons of men, their teeth are arms and arrows; and elsewhere: His words are softer than oil, and yet they are darts; and more openly in Ecclesiastes: If a serpent bite in silence, so is he who secretly disparages his brother. But you say: "I myself do not disparage; what can I do when others speak?" These things we hold out to excuse our excuses in sins. Christ is not mocked by craft. By no means is it my sentence, but the Apostle's: Do not err; God is not mocked. He sees in the heart, we in the face. Solomon says in the Proverbs: The north wind scatters clouds, and a sad face the tongues of disparagers. For just as an arrow, if it be shot against a hard material, sometimes returns upon the shooter and wounds the wounder, and that is fulfilled: They were turned to me into a crooked bow; and elsewhere: He who casts a stone on high, it will fall back upon his head — so the disparager, when he sees the sad face of the hearer — nay, not even of the hearer, but of one stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood — at once falls silent, his face grows pale, his lips cling together, his saliva dries up. Whence the same wise man says: Do not mingle with disparagers, for their destruction shall come suddenly; and the ruin of both, who knows it? — namely, both of him who speaks and of him who hears the speaker. Truth does not love corners nor seek whisperers. To Timothy it is said: Against a presbyter do not quickly receive an accusation. But him who sins reprove before all, that the rest also may have fear. It is not easy to believe of the perfect age, which both a past life defends and the title of dignity honours; but, since we are men and sometimes, against the maturity of our years, slip into the vices of boys, if you wish me to be corrected when I offend, rebuke me openly, only do not bite me secretly: The just man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives. And through Isaiah God cries: My people, they who call you blessed seduce you and overturn the paths of your feet. For what does it profit me if you report my evils to others, if, without my knowing, you wound another with my sins — nay, with your detractions — and, while you eagerly tell all, so speak to each one as though you had told no other? This is not to amend me, but to satisfy your own vice. The Lord commands that those who sin against us ought to be reproved in secret, or with a witness called in, and, if they refuse to hear, to be referred to the Church, and those obstinate in evil to be held as heathens and publicans.

20. These things I speak more expressly, that I may free my young man from the itch both of the tongue and of the ears, that, reborn in Christ, I may present him without wrinkle and spot, like a chaste virgin, and holy both in mind and body, lest he glory in the name alone and, the lamp quenched, without the oil of good works, be shut out from the Bridegroom. You have there the holy and most learned bishop Proculus, who with living and present voice may surpass my sheets and direct your way with daily discourses, and not suffer you, by turning aside to the one side or the other, to leave the royal road, by which Israel, hastening to the land of promise, promises that it will pass. And would that the voice of the Church, lamenting together, were heard: Lord, give us peace, for you have rendered all things to us. Would that what we renounce of the world were a matter of will, not of necessity, and that poverty had the glory of being sought, not the torment of being imposed. But, according to the miseries of this time and the swords raging everywhere, he is rich enough who does not lack bread, too powerful who is not compelled to serve. The holy Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, an imitator of the widow of Sarepta, hungering feeds others, and with patient mouth is tortured by another's fasting and famine, and has spent all his substance on the bowels of Christ. Nothing is richer than he who carries the body of the Lord in a wicker basket, the blood in glass, who has cast avarice out of the temple, who, without a scourge and the rebuke of those selling doves — that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit — overturned the tables of mammon and scattered the money of the money-changers, that the house of God might be called a house of prayer and not a den of robbers. Follow from nearby his footsteps, and those of the others who are like his virtues, whom the priesthood makes both humbler and poorer; or, if you desire perfect things, go out with Abraham from your country and from your kindred, and go where you know not. If you have substance, sell it and give to the poor; if you have it not, you are freed from a great burden; naked, follow the naked Christ. Hard, great, difficult — but the rewards are great.

1. It is a difficult business to write to a little girl who does not understand what you say, whose soul you do not know, of whose will you make promises at peril — so that, according to the opening of a distinguished orator, the hope in her is more to be praised than the reality. For why should you exhort to continence one who longs for cakes, who babbles with prattling voice in her mother's lap, to whom honey is sweeter than words? Should she hear the deep things of the Apostle, who is delighted rather by old wives' tales? Should she perceive the riddles of the prophets, whom the sadder face of her bearer frightens off? Should she understand the majesty of the Gospel, at whose lightnings every sense of mortals was dulled? Should I exhort her to be subject to her parent, who with tender hand strikes her laughing mother? Therefore let our Pacatula receive this little letter to read afterward; for the present let her only learn the elements of the little letters, join syllables, learn nouns, link words together; and, that she may rehearse these with ringing voice, let a little cake of honey be set before her as a reward, and let her hasten to take whatever is sweet to the taste, whatever blooms in flowers, whatever glows in gems, whatever charms in dolls; meanwhile let her also try with her tender thumb to draw out the threads, let her often break the strands, that one day she may not break them; after labour let her exult in play, let her hang from her mother's neck, let her snatch the kisses of her kinsfolk, let her sing psalms for a reward, let her love what she is compelled to say, that it may be not a task but a delight, not a necessity but a wish.

2. Some, when they have promised a future virgin, are wont to clothe her in a dark tunic and cover her with a black little cloak, to take away the linens, to allow no gold on the neck, none on the head — with good counsel indeed, lest she learn to have in her tender years what afterward she may be compelled to lay aside. To others the opposite seems best. "For what," they say, "if she herself has not had it, will she not see others who have?" The female sex is fond of adornment, and we know that many even of distinguished chastity, though for no man, yet for themselves, gladly deck themselves out. Nay rather, let her be sated by having, and see others praised who do not have these things. And it is better that, being sated, she should despise them, than that, not having them, she should desire to have them. The Lord did something of the kind too for the people of Israel, when, to those longing for the flesh of Egypt, he furnished swarms of quails even to nausea and vomiting; and many men of the world have by experience more easily done without the pleasure of the body than those who from boyhood know nothing of lust; for things known are trampled by the one, things unknown sought by the other; the former by repenting avoid the snares of sweetness which they fled, the latter are caught by the allurements of the flesh and the sweet titillation of the body's flattery, while they think to find honey and discover noxious poisons; for honey distils from the lips of a harlot woman, which for a time fattens the throats of those who eat it, and afterward is found bitterer than gall. Hence too honey is not offered in the Lord's sacrifices, and the wax, which is the lodging of honey, being despised, oil is kindled in the temple of God, which is pressed out from the bitterness of olives; the Passover too is eaten with bitter herbs, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and whoever has these will endure persecution in the world. Hence too the prophet mystically sings: I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness.

3. What then? Must one revel in youth, that afterward luxury may be more strongly despised? "God forbid," they say; For let each one, in the calling in which he was called, in that abide.
Is anyone called circumcised — that is, a virgin? Let him not draw on the foreskin — that is, let him not seek the skin-tunics of marriage, with which Adam, cast out of the paradise of virginity, was clothed. Is anyone called in the foreskin — that is, having a wife and girded about with the skin of matrimony? Let him not seek the nakedness of virginity and eternal chastity, which he has once ceased to have, but let him use his own vessel in sanctification and chastity, and drink from his own fountains, and not seek the shattered cisterns of the brothels, which cannot contain the purest waters of chastity. Hence too the same Paul, in the same chapter, disputing of virginity and marriage, calls those constituted in matrimony servants of the flesh, and free those who, without any yoke of marriage, serve the Lord with all liberty.
What we say, we say not of all in general, but treat in part, nor speak of all, but of certain ones. Our discourse is directed to both sexes, not to the weaker vessel only. You are a virgin: why does the society of a woman delight you? Why do you commit a frail and patched raft to the great waves, and, secure, embark on the great peril of an uncertain voyage? You know not what you desire, and yet you so join yourself to her as though you had either desired before or — to speak most lightly — would desire afterward. "But that sex is more fit for service." Choose, then, an old woman; choose a deformed one; choose one of proved continence in the Lord. Why does a young one delight you, why a beautiful one, why a luxurious one? You use the baths, with shining skin, you walk about ruddy, you feed on flesh, you abound in riches, surrounded with precious garments, and do you believe that you sleep secure next to a deadly serpent? Or do you not dwell in the same lodging — at night at least? But spending whole days in conversation of this kind, why do you, alone with a woman alone, sit and not with witnesses? Even though you yourself do not sin, you may seem to others to sin, so that you are an example to the wretched, who by the authority of your name may transgress. You too, virgin or widow, why do you detain a man with so long a discourse? Why, left alone with one alone, do you not fear? At least let the necessity of the bowels and the bladder compel you to go out, that you may leave him, with whom in this matter, more freely than with a brother, far more modestly you have acted than with a husband. "But you ask something of the Holy Scriptures": ask in public; let your maids hear, let your companions hear. Everything that is made manifest is light. Good speech does not seek secret places; nay rather, it delights in its own praises and the testimony of very many. The excellent master despises men, scorns brothers, and sweats over the secret instruction of one little woman.

4. I have turned a little from the way on the occasion of others, and, while I instruct the infant Pacatula — nay, nourish her — I have suddenly taken up wars with many women ill at peace with me. I will return to my purpose. Let the female sex be joined to its own sex; let her not know — nay, let her fear — to play with boys. Let her know no unchaste word, and, if perchance in the tumult of the bustling household she hear anything foul, let her not understand it. Let her have her mother's nod for words and her warning for a command. Let her love her as a parent, be subject to her as a mistress, fear her as a teacher. But when the seventh year of her age has received the little maiden, still untaught and toothless, and she has begun to blush, to know what to keep silent, to be in doubt what to say, let her learn the psalter by heart, and until the years of puberty let her make the books of Solomon, the gospels, the apostles, and the prophets the treasure of her heart. Let her not go out too freely into public, nor always seek the gatherings of the churches. Let her have all her delights in her own chamber. Let her never see young men, never curled fellows wounding the soul through the ears with sweetness of voice. The wantonness of girls too is to be repelled, who, the more freely they approach, the more difficultly they are avoided, and who teach in secret what they have learned, and violate a shut-in Danaë by the talk of the crowd. Let her teacher be a companion, her tutor a guardian, not much given to wine, not, according to the Apostle, idle and wordy, but sober, grave, a worker of wool, and speaking only those things which instruct the minds of girls to virtue. But as water in a little channel follows the finger going before it, so the soft and tender age is flexible to either side, and is drawn wherever you lead it. Wanton and trim young men are wont to seek for themselves, through the nurses, an approach to the foster-children by blandishments, affability, and little gifts, and, when they have gently entered, to rouse fires from sparks and gradually to advance to shamelessness, and to be by no means able to be prevented, that little verse being proved upon them: You can hardly find fault with what you allow to become a habit. It is shameful to say, and yet it must be said: noble women, destined to have nobler suitors, are coupled with men of the cheapest condition and with servants, and, under the name of religion and the shadow of continence, sometimes desert their husbands. They are Helens following Alexanders, and do not fear the Menelauses. These things are seen, are lamented, and are not avenged, because the multitude of those who sin supplies the license of sinning.

5. Oh, the wickedness! The world is falling to ruin, and in us our sins do not fall. The renowned city, the head of the Roman Empire, has been swallowed up by one conflagration. There is no region that does not have its exiles. Churches once sacred have fallen into ashes and embers, and yet we are zealous for avarice. We live as though about to die the next day, and we build as though always about to live in this world. The walls gleam with gold, the panelled ceilings with gold, the capitals of the columns shine with gold, and naked and hungry before our doors Christ dies in the person of the poor. We read that Aaron the high priest went to meet the raging flames, and, the censer kindled, checked the wrath of God; the great priest stood between death and life, and the fire dared not advance beyond his footsteps. God says to Moses: Let me alone, and I will destroy this people. When he says "Let me alone," he shows that he is held back from doing what he had threatened; for the servant's prayers were hindering the power of God. Who, do you think, is there under heaven who could now meet the wrath of God, who could go to meet the flames and, with the Apostle, say: I myself wished to be anathema for my brethren? The flocks perish with the shepherds, because, as the people, so the priest. Moses spoke with the affection of compassion: If you forgive this people, forgive; but if not, blot me out of your book. He wishes to perish with those who perish, nor is he content with his own salvation. For the glory of a king is the multitude of his people.
In these times Pacatula was born; amid these rattles she snatches her first age, destined to know tears before laughter, to feel weeping before joy. Scarcely has she entered, and already is the exit; she thinks the world has always been such. She knows not the past, she flees the present, she desires the future. That I should dictate these things in hasty speech, and that I, an old man, should write to an infant, after the deaths of friends and perpetual mourning, by a long return from exile, your love, brother Gaudentius, impelled me; and to give my hand to one asking less than nothing at all — because in the one case the will is oppressed by grief, in the other there is a dissembling of friendship.
